elpis ἐλπίς elpis — hope, confident expectation Feminine noun. Accusative singular: elpida (ἐλπίδα). Denotes absolute confidence and total assurance with respect to future things. In biblical usage, incompatible with ignorance or uncertainty. The sole source of biblical hope is the perception of Bible doctrine.
elpizō ἐλπίζω elpizō — to hope, to have confident expectation Cognate verb of elpis. To place confident expectation in a future divine reality. Not wishful thinking but informed, doctrine-based assurance.
echō ἔχω echō — to have, to have and to hold Present active subjunctive: echōmen (ἔχωμεν). The perfective present tense notes the continuation of existing results — the believer who has persevered in doctrine possesses hope as a stable, ongoing state of soul.
hina ἵνα hina — in order that Subordinating conjunction introducing a purpose clause. Governs the subjunctive echōmen in Romans 15:4, marking the possessing of hope as the stated purpose of all preceding activity — perseverance in and comfort from the Scriptures.
midbat / kesel מִדְבַּת / כֶּסֶל midbat / kesel — Hebrew terms for hope Two of the principal Hebrew vocabulary items translated 'hope' in the Old Testament. Both denote confident expectation directed toward a specific future reality, corresponding to the Greek elpis in semantic range.
Protocol Plan of God The overarching divine framework governing human history, the angelic conflict, and the believer's operational life in the Church Age. Establishes the authorized procedures by which God acts toward mankind and by which believers function within His plan.
Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) The Spirit-enabled process by which the believer receives, understands, and internalizes Bible doctrine. Requires the filling of the Holy Spirit, a qualified human teacher, and positive volition on the part of the recipient.
Royal Family Honor Code The standard of conduct governing Church Age believers in their relationship to God, to fellow believers, and to unbelievers. Grounded in the believer's identity as a member of the royal family of God; includes flexibility with respect to non-essentials, impersonal love, and respect for the privacy of the believer-priest.
Indigenous missionary principle The missiological standard by which a receiving church is established as self-governing, self-supporting, and self-propagating from the outset, without dependence on foreign financing or foreign leadership. Formalized by Dr. John Nevius for the Korean mission in 1890 and documented as the framework of the Korean revival of 1890–1915.

Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Four

Romans 15:4 — Doctrine of Hope: Points 3–8 — The Three Categories of Hope in the Plan of God

Romans 15:4 “For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For as many doctrines as have been written before, for our instruction they were written, in order that through perseverance and encouragement from the Scriptures we might have hope.

Romans 15:1–4 has established the foundation of the Royal Family Honor Code, showing that the mature believer bears the weaknesses of the immature, accommodates his neighbor for edification, and follows the example of Christ, who absorbed the insults directed at the Father. The final phrase of verse 4 — 'that through perseverance and encouragement from the Scriptures we might have hope' — introduces a sustained study of the doctrine of hope. This chapter covers points three through eight of that doctrine, culminating in the three categories of hope embedded in the equation of the plan of God.

I. Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God

The third point of the doctrine of hope is this: hope anticipates the function of the integrity of God. All three categories of hope in the plan of God are anchored not in human ability, social achievement, or military greatness, but in the integrity of God — specifically in His righteousness and His justice working in concert on the believer's behalf.

Hope is not the same as wish or optimism. Hope, in the biblical sense, is confident anticipation of a future reality that has not yet occurred but is guaranteed by the character of God. This confidence is not innate to the human soul. It must be cultivated through consistent intake of Bible doctrine.

1 Thessalonians 1:3 anchors this point precisely: "constantly bearing in mind your work of doctrine and labor of love and courage under pressure... from hope in our Lord Jesus Christ in the presence of God the Father." The three great characteristics of the mature believer — work of doctrine, impersonal love, and courage under pressure — all flow from a single source: hope in Christ. Doctrine produces the hope, and the hope produces the life.

Job 4:6 reinforces this: "Is not your respect for God your confidence? Is not your hope the integrity of your ways?" The integrity of the believer's life in time is itself the product of hope — and that hope is grounded in the integrity of God, not in any human virtue.

Psalm 71:5 expresses the mature believer's orientation: "For you are my hope, O Lord God, my confidence from my youth." David's greatness as a man of God — despite personal failures, foibles, and the full weight of his old sin nature — rested on this structured confidence in the integrity of God. Doctrine parlayed into a systematized system of soul confidence is what Scripture calls hope.

Jeremiah 17:7 adds the connection to the faith-rest technique: "Blessed is the man who puts his trust in the Lord, and whose hope is in the Lord." In the immature believer, this confidence operates as faith-rest. In the mature believer, sustained doctrine intake has transformed faith-rest into a structurized system of anticipatory confidence — which is hope in its full biblical sense.

Romans 4:18 presents Abraham as the paradigm case: who "beyond hope believed in hope" — that is, beyond any human basis for confidence, Abraham's confidence was anchored in the integrity of God. The physical fulfillment of the promise came as a point of undeserved suffering when Abraham was entirely beyond natural expectation. Hope held because its object was not circumstance but divine integrity.

II. Point 4 — God Is the Author of Hope; Doctrine Is Its Source

God is the author of hope, but He does not dispense hope apart from doctrine. Hope is not distributed indiscriminately. It is the product of learning, receiving, and internalizing the Word of God through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). Romans 15:4 makes this explicit: the Scriptures were written for our instruction, and it is through perseverance in that instruction that hope is produced.

Hebrews 11:1 grounds this further: "Doctrine is the reality from which we receive hope, the proof of matters not being seen." Hope is not detached from content. It is doctrine that gives hope its substance, its precision, and its forward momentum. Without doctrine, the soul has potential — the grace provisions are objectively in place — but it does not have hope, because hope requires perception.

The distinction between potential and hope is critical: potential is what God has provided by grace; hope is what the believer possesses by perception. Every reversionist and apostate believer has the potential of blessing, but not the hope — because between potential and hope stands doctrine. The reversionist has rejected the instrument of perception. The potential is there, but it remains inert.

III. Points 5–6 — The Equation of the Plan of God and Three Categories of Hope

The Structural Equation

The plan of God may be expressed as a three-part equation in which each radical contains two imputations, a resulting potential, pertinent doctrine, and a corresponding hope. The equation is X + Y + Z = the plan of God. Each radical moves the believer forward through a distinct metamorphism. The three hopes are the momentum factors that drive that advance.

X Radical — The First Hope

X radical is God's plan for the entire human race prior to salvation. It contains two imputations at physical birth: human life imputed to the soul, and Adam's original sin imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. These two imputations result in simultaneous condemnation, which is the necessary precondition for salvation. Condemnation must precede salvation.

This condemnation establishes the first potential: the potential of eternal salvation. Between the potential and the hope stands pertinent doctrine — specifically the gospel. God the Holy Spirit functions as a surrogate human spirit for the unbeliever, making the gospel perceivable through the ministry of common grace. When the unbeliever hears, understands, and acts on the gospel — inhaling the content, exhaling faith in Christ — hope one becomes reality.

Romans 8:24 states: "Now when a hope is seen, it is no longer a hope; so who hopes for what he sees?" Once the reality of salvation occurs, the first hope is replaced by that reality. The momentum of the plan of God has produced its first metamorphism: the unbeliever becomes a believer.

Hebrews 7:19 designates this as "a better hope, through which we draw near to God." Titus 1:2 traces it to the divine decrees: "in hope of eternal life, which God who cannot lie promised before times eternal." Titus 3:7 confirms the result: "being justified by His grace, that we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life."

Job 5:16 summarizes the scope of the first hope: "the helpless have hope." Positive volition at God-consciousness guarantees the opportunity of gospel hearing. Common grace converting to efficacious grace is the mechanism. No one is excluded from this hope by circumstance, background, or moral condition.

Y Radical — The Second Hope

Y radical contains two judicial imputations. The first is the imputation of all personal sins to Christ at the cross, where they were judged. The second is the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at the moment of salvation. These two imputations establish the second potential: the potential of great blessing imputed in time as the means by which the believer glorifies Jesus Christ in history.

Between the potential and the second hope stands pertinent doctrine — the full range of post-salvation biblical teaching covering the protocol plan of God, the Royal Family Honor Code, the doctrine of adjustment to the justice of God, and the mechanics of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). The second hope is absolute confidence that when the believer cracks the maturity barrier — through daily function of GAP with perseverance — six categories of blessing will be imputed directly by God. These blessings glorify the Lord Jesus Christ in time and constitute the reality of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

When the maturity barrier is cracked and the believer enters supergrace A, supergrace B, or ultra-supergrace, the second hope is replaced by its reality. The blessing is no longer a confident anticipation — it is a present possession. The plan of God advances to its third radical.

Z Radical — The Third Hope

Z radical contains two final imputations. Eternal life, imputed at salvation, provides the basis for resurrection existence. The imputation of blessing in time — the reality that replaced the second hope — provides the basis for evaluation at the judgment seat of Christ. These two imputations establish the third potential: great blessing and reward forever, which glorifies God eternally.

Between the third potential and the third hope stands pertinent doctrine plus undeserved suffering. Undeserved suffering in the post-maturity life of the mature believer is not punitive. It is the divine mechanism by which ultra-supergrace capacity is deepened and eternal reward is intensified. The third hope is absolute confidence that after the rapture of the church, at the judgment seat of Christ, the mature believer will receive the imputation of great blessing and reward that glorifies God forever.

Romans 15:13 anticipates the third hope in its fullest expression: "May the God of hope fill you with all happiness and prosperity in believing, that you may super-abound in the third hope by the power of the Holy Spirit." This is hope as superabundance — the distinctive possession of the mature believer in the Church Age.

IV. Points 7–8 — Imputation as the Basis of Hope; Doctrine as the Differentiator

Point 7 — Imputation Is the Basis for Each Hope

In each of the three radicals, two imputations provide both the potential and the structural basis for the corresponding hope. This is not incidental. Imputation is the mechanism by which God acts directly and immediately on the believer's behalf without the mediation of human merit, effort, or social position. Every hope in the plan of God rests on an imputation — an act of the justice of God crediting something to someone's account.

The critical observation from the equation is that doctrine appears three times on the right side — once in each radical, between the potential and the hope. Potential is grace. Hope is the product of perception. The same grace provisions are available to every believer. The mature believer and the reversionist share the same potential. What differentiates them is doctrine resident in the soul.

Doctrine resident in the soul through the function of GAP makes the difference between potential and hope. A potential is not an advance in the plan of God. It is doctrine that advances the believer. The reversionist has the potential of blessing but not the hope, because he has rejected the instrument of perception. The mature believer has both — and when the hope is replaced by its reality, two new imputations come into view and the momentum of the plan continues.

Point 8 — Hope Is the Momentum Factor in the Plan of God

Hope is not static. It is always forward-looking, always pressing toward a future reality that is guaranteed by the integrity of God. Once a hope becomes reality, it must be set aside — because hope, by definition, looks ahead. The plan of God is structured so that the believer is never without a hope. When one hope is replaced by its reality, the new imputations of the next radical immediately establish the next hope.

Romans 8:24 is the governing principle: "For with reference to that hope, we have been saved." The first hope was the instrument of momentum that carried the unbeliever into salvation. The second hope carries the believer through the post-salvation life toward maturity. The third hope carries the mature believer through undeserved suffering toward resurrection and eternal reward. At every stage, hope is the engine.

Ephesians 2:12 describes the condition of the unbeliever with precision: no hope in this world. Hope in the biblical sense is not a general human capacity. It belongs to the believer by virtue of the imputations of God and the perception of doctrine. Every believer has at least the first hope. The mature believer possesses all three in sequence — and the third hope, the superabounding confidence of the ultra-supergrace believer, is the distinctive glory of the Church Age plan of God.

The three hopes together constitute the full momentum of the Christian life. All thrust in the Christian life is based upon them. When hope is replaced by reality at each stage, the believer does not stall — two new imputations immediately set up a new thrust. This is the design of the plan of God: not a single leap but a structured, sequential advance driven by imputation, enabled by doctrine, and expressed as hope.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Four

1. Hope is confident anticipation of a future reality: not wish, not optimism, and not mere possibility. It is structured confidence about something that has not yet occurred but is guaranteed by the character of God. This confidence is the product of doctrine resident in the soul.

2. Hope anticipates the function of the integrity of God: all three categories of hope are anchored in the righteousness and justice of God acting on the believer's behalf. No category of hope is grounded in human ability, social standing, or natural talent.

3. God is the author of hope; doctrine is its source: God does not distribute hope apart from the Word. Between every divine potential and its corresponding hope stands doctrine — specifically, the believer's perception of that doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

4. Potential is not hope: every believer — including the reversionist and the apostate — possesses the potential of divine blessing. Only the believer who is advancing in doctrine possesses the corresponding hope. Doctrine is the differentiating factor.

5. The plan of God contains three sequential hopes: Hope 1 — confident anticipation of salvation through faith in Christ (X radical). Hope 2 — confident anticipation of the imputation of blessing in time at the maturity barrier (Y radical). Hope 3 — confident anticipation of eternal blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ (Z radical).

6. Imputation is the structural basis for each hope: two imputations in each radical provide both the potential and the hope. The imputations are acts of the justice of God — direct, non-meritorious credits to the believer's account that establish the objective ground for confident anticipation.

7. Once reality replaces a hope, momentum continues: when one hope is fulfilled, the plan of God does not pause. The new imputations of the next radical immediately establish a new hope and a new forward thrust. The believer is never left without a hope toward which to press.

8. Hope is the momentum factor in the plan of God: all spiritual advance — from salvation through maturity to eternal reward — is driven by hope. The superabounding hope of Romans 15:13, produced by the power of the Holy Spirit, is the distinctive possession of the ultra-supergrace believer and the capstone of the Church Age plan.

9. Common grace converts to efficacious grace through the first hope: God the Holy Spirit presents the gospel to the unbeliever at positive volition, making it perceptible as epignosis. The unbeliever who understands the gospel possesses hope one. The exhale of faith in Christ replaces that hope with the reality of salvation — the first metamorphism in the plan of God.

10. The third hope is the superabounding confidence of the mature believer: Romans 15:13 addresses this hope directly. It is produced by the power of the Holy Spirit in the soul that has advanced through maximum doctrine intake, undeserved suffering, and sustained adjustment to the justice of God. It is the forward momentum carrying the mature believer toward resurrection, the judgment seat of Christ, and eternal glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
hope ἐλπίς elpis — hope, confident expectation In biblical usage, confident anticipation of a future reality that has not yet occurred but is guaranteed by the integrity of God. Distinguished from mere optimism by its doctrinal content and divine grounding. Always forward-looking; replaced by reality when the anticipated event occurs.
epignosis ἐπίγνωσις epignosis — full, exact knowledge The category of knowledge required for spiritual advance. Distinguished from gnosis (academic acquaintance) by the transfer of doctrine from the written Word to the human spirit and right lobe of the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Epignosis alone converts potential into hope.
GAP — Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is received, understood, and transferred to the right lobe of the soul as epignosis. Requires consistent, daily intake under the ministry of God the Holy Spirit. The instrument that converts divine potential into the believer's operative hope.
adjustment to the justice of God δικαιοσύνη θεοφ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The central organizing principle of Romans. All divine blessing flows through the justice of God. Three stages: (1) salvation adjustment — faith in Christ; (2) rebound adjustment — naming known sins to God (1 John 1:9); (3) maturity adjustment — progressive doctrine intake culminating in supergrace.
imputation λογίζομαι logizomai — to reckon, to credit to an account The direct crediting of something to a person's account by divine act, apart from human merit. Six imputations structure the plan of God: human life and Adam's sin at birth; all personal sins to Christ at the cross and divine righteousness at salvation; eternal life at salvation and blessing at maturity. Imputation is the structural basis for each of the three hopes.
maturity barrier The threshold of spiritual maturity cracked through sustained daily doctrine intake over time. Cracking the maturity barrier is the prerequisite for the imputation of the six categories of blessing in time that constitute the reality of the second hope. The believer who crosses it enters supergrace A, progressing toward supergrace B and ultra-supergrace.
supergrace / ultra-supergrace Stages of spiritual maturity beyond the maturity barrier. Supergrace A and B describe the progressive reception of divine blessing in time through direct imputation from the justice of God. Ultra-supergrace describes the highest stage, characterized by superabounding hope (Romans 15:13) and intensified eternal reward through undeserved suffering.
common grace The ministry of God the Holy Spirit by which the gospel is made perceptible to the unbeliever. Because the unbeliever lacks a human spirit, he cannot understand spiritual phenomena unaided. The Holy Spirit acts as a surrogate human spirit, presenting the gospel as epignosis. Common grace becomes efficacious grace when the unbeliever exercises faith in Christ.
faith-rest The technique by which the believer claims a divine promise under pressure and rests in its certainty. In the immature believer, the primary mechanism of trust. In the mature believer, sustained doctrine intake transforms faith-rest into a structurized system of confident anticipation — which Scripture designates as hope.
reversionism Retroactive spiritual regression — the believer returning to the values, thinking, and orientation of the old sin nature. The reversionist retains the objective potential of divine blessing but has rejected the instrument of perception (doctrine) and therefore does not possess the corresponding hope. The potential is inert without the hope.

Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Five

Romans 15:1–4 — The Doctrine of Hope: Points 9–13

Romans 15:4 “For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For as many as have been written before — many doctrines from the Old Testament — for our instruction they were written, in order that through perseverance and encouragement from the Scriptures we might have hope.

Romans 15 continues the exposition of the honor code binding mature believers toward those who are weaker in doctrine. Verses 1 through 4 have been completed in preceding chapters. The present chapter resumes the doctrine of hope at point 9, the second hope in the three-hope equation, and proceeds through point 13. The controlling motif is the same one that runs through all of Romans: adjustment to the justice of God as the exclusive mechanism through which divine blessing reaches the believer.

I. The Three-Hope Equation — Review of Structure

The doctrine of hope in Romans 15:4 is organized around three distinct hopes, each corresponding to a stage in the believer's advance through the Protocol Plan of God. The first hope (X-radical) was treated in the preceding chapter and concerns the imputation of human life plus Adam's original sin at birth, establishing the first potential, which combined with doctrine produces hope one. The present chapter takes up the second and third hopes.

The organizing logic is consistent throughout. Between every potential and its corresponding hope stands doctrine — specifically, Bible doctrine resident in the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). Without the intake and perception of doctrine, potential remains potential and never becomes hope. This is not a human achievement but the consistent operation of divine integrity: righteousness as the principle, justice as the function.

II. Point 9 — The Second Hope (Y-Radical)

A. The Two Judicial Imputations

The second hope is grounded in two judicial imputations. The first judicial imputation is the imputation of all the sins of the world to Christ on the cross (illustrated in Romans 15:2). The second judicial imputation is the imputation of divine righteousness to every believer at the moment of salvation. This second judicial imputation is the pivotal event that makes the entire advance to maturity possible.

The second judicial imputation produces the second potential: the potential of glorifying God in time, and the potential of receiving the imputation of divine blessing in time. This potential differs categorically from any form of human security, which is always precarious and always accompanied by the anxiety of possible loss. The second potential, by contrast, is grounded in the justice of God, which can only bless what it has itself established — namely, divine righteousness imputed at salvation (dikaiosynē theou, δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ).

B. Doctrine Transforms Potential into Hope

Between the second potential and the second hope stands doctrine. The second hope is absolute confidence that by persevering in the daily intake of Bible doctrine, the believer will attain maturity adjustment to the justice of God. This is not wishful thinking. It is structural certainty rooted in the character of God: divine justice cannot withhold blessing from divine righteousness, and the believer possesses divine righteousness by judicial imputation. The advance is therefore guaranteed at the level of divine integrity, conditioned only on the believer's positive volition toward doctrine.

In the Church Age, the believer possesses a double portion of divine righteousness: the imputed righteousness received at salvation, and the shared righteousness of Christ received through the baptism of the Holy Spirit at salvation (union with Christ). This double portion establishes a grace pipeline between the justice of God and the righteousness of God resident in the believer. Divine blessing travels that pipeline when the believer has advanced sufficiently in doctrine to have capacity for what is imputed.

C. The Advance from Salvation to Maturity

The second hope governs the entire momentum phase of the Christian life. At salvation the believer receives imputed righteousness (plus R). The objective of phase two is to advance from that starting point to maturity, so that divine blessing can be imputed to plus R from the justice of God. The stages are: crack the maturity barrier (supergrace A), advance through supergrace A to supergrace B, and then to ultra-supergrace, the apex of spiritual attainment in time. The categories of blessing imputed at and beyond the maturity barrier are six in number and represent the fulfillment of imputed righteousness.

The critical axiom is this: divine justice can only bless divine righteousness. God does not dispense blessing on the basis of human talent, personality, social achievement, emotional sincerity, or external religious performance. Blessing is the precise operation of perfect justice imputing to perfect righteousness. Capacity — the ability to receive and enjoy divine blessing without anxiety or misuse — is produced exclusively by doctrine resident in the soul. Without capacity, blessing produces misery rather than happiness. This is why logistical grace provision is withheld at the higher levels until the believer has developed the doctrinal capacity to receive and use it for glorification of God rather than for self-centered hoarding or compulsive anxiety.

D. Scriptural Documentation of the Second Hope

Lamentations 3:21–25 provides the classical Old Testament exposition of the second hope. Verse 21: 'This I recall to mind, therefore I have hope' — the second hope arising from maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Verse 22: 'The Lord's gracious functions never cease, for His compassions never fail' — logistical grace support, which becomes the base for greater blessing at the maturity barrier. Verse 23: 'They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness' — the faithfulness of divine integrity sustaining the believer through every stage of advance. Verse 24: 'The Lord is my portion, says my soul, therefore I have hope in Him' — the second hope resting on the character of God rather than on human circumstance. Verse 25: 'The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him' — perseverance and positive volition toward doctrine as the condition of advance.

Second Corinthians 10:15 states the principle directly: 'Not boasting beyond our measure in other men's labors, but with the hope that as your doctrine increases, we shall be within our sphere enlarged even more.' The enlargement of spiritual sphere is proportional to doctrinal increase — this is the second hope as motivation for continued advance.

Galatians 5:5 completes the documentation: 'For we through the Spirit, from doctrine, are waiting for the hope of righteousness.' The phrase hope of righteousness refers to the fact that imputed righteousness demands fulfillment through the imputation of divine blessing at the point of maturity and thereafter. Imputed righteousness is not an end in itself but a standing order — a guarantee that justice will act when capacity is in place.

Matthew 6:33 implies the second hope: 'Seek first the kingdom and His imputed righteousness, and all these things will be provided for you.' Romans 5:1 commands it: 'Therefore having been justified by faith, let us have prosperity' — the imputation of divine blessing as a commanded expectation grounded in justification. Romans 5:17 presents the second hope within the doctrine of the second category of the overflow of blessing.

First Peter 3:15 gives the pastoral application: 'Set apart Christ as Lord of your right lobes. Always be ready to give a reason to everyone who asks you to give an account for the hope that is in you.' The hope referenced is the second hope — the absolute confidence of advancing to maturity and receiving the imputation of divine blessing.

E. The Second Hope as Both Confidence and Motivation

The second hope functions in two directions simultaneously. As confidence, it provides the mature assurance that the advance to maturity is guaranteed at the level of divine integrity — provided the believer maintains positive volition toward doctrine. As motivation, it provides the momentum principle that sustains daily doctrine intake: knowing that blessing is imputed only at and beyond the maturity barrier, the believer has structural incentive to continue advancing. The only legitimate Christian function that produces blessing is the intake of doctrine. All other legitimate functions — prayer, witness, service — produce spiritual production but not the direct imputation of divine blessing from justice to righteousness.

III. Point 10 — The Third Hope (Z-Radical)

A. Structure of the Third Potential

The third hope is constructed from: mental life imputed at salvation to the human spirit, plus blessing in time imputed at maturity to the believer's imputed righteousness, equals the third potential. The third potential is the potential for great blessing at the judgment seat of Christ in eternity. The third potential plus doctrine plus undeserved suffering equals the third hope.

The third hope is the hope with which the mature believer lives and dies. It is the highest structural and dynamic thinking that can occupy the soul of the believer in time. It is always correlated with two other factors: doctrine resident in the soul, and undeserved suffering. The mature believer is always blessed in undeserved suffering because suffering provides the impetus and stimulation that deepen the third hope and increase momentum through phase two. Dying grace is inseparable from the third hope: Abraham died in a tent, yet Hebrews 11 records that he lived in confident anticipation of the city whose builder and maker is God.

B. The Third Hope and the Rapture Generation

A natural question arises concerning believers whose advance toward maturity is interrupted by the rapture. The omniscience of God knows not only what occurs but what would have occurred under any counterfactual condition. The justice of God is incapable of unfairness. Therefore, a believer who is positive toward doctrine at the point of the rapture receives blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ based on the trajectory of advance that the omniscience of God knows would have been completed. Conversely, consistent negative volition toward doctrine at the time of the rapture is also taken into account with full precision. There is no randomness and no injustice at the judgment seat of Christ.

C. Scriptural Documentation of the Third Hope

Acts 23:6 records Paul's declaration before the Sanhedrin: 'I am on trial for the hope, even the resurrection from the dead.' The hope in view is the third hope. Paul repeats the identification in Acts 24:15 and Acts 26:6. The third hope is explicitly resurrection hope — confidence that the resurrection body will be the vehicle for the imputation of eternal blessing and reward.

Romans 12:12 provides the command: 'With reference to the hope — be rejoicing.' The hope here is the third hope, and it is the source of joy for the mature believer in the midst of the pressures of life.

Ephesians 1:18–19 contains both the second and third hopes. Colossians 1:5 locates the third hope in heaven as a reserved inheritance: 'Because of the hope laid up for you in heaven, of which you previously heard in the word of truth.' Titus 2:13 frames the third hope eschatologically: 'Looking for that blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God, even our Savior Christ Jesus.'

First Peter 1:3 defines the trajectory from salvation to the third hope: 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to His great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.' First Peter 1:13 commands the orientation: 'Gird your minds for action, be constantly stabilized and oriented, fix your hope on the grace being brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.' First Peter 1:21 anchors the hope in the resurrection and glorification of Christ: 'So that your faith and your hope are in God.'

Hebrews 6:18–20 provides the fullest analysis of the third hope in terms of divine integrity: 'In order that by two immutable things — God's oath and His promise — in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have strong encouragement, we who have fled for refuge in doctrine for the purpose of attaining the hope set before us. Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both secure and dependable, and one which enters into the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus, the forerunner, has entered on our behalf, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.' Christ as forerunner and high priest establishes the pattern: resurrection body, entrance into the presence of God, reception of the third category of royalty as the spoils of strategic victory in the angelic conflict. The mature believer anticipates all of this through the third hope.

First John 3:2–3 states the purifying effect of the third hope: 'Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we will be. But we know that when He appears, we will be like Him, because we will see Him just as He is. And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as He is pure.' The possession of the third hope motivates purity of motivation and perpetuates spiritual momentum. The third hope is not merely an eschatological datum but a present operational dynamic in the soul of the mature believer.

D. The Third Hope and the Overflow of Blessing

The third hope is the final stage of the second category of the overflow of divine blessing, a doctrine treated in detail in Romans 5:17. The logic is stated as an inference from the greater to the less: if the justice of God imputed the greater blessing at spiritual maturity in time, then it follows that the justice of God will also impute the less — eternal blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ — to the resurrection body of the mature believer. The imputation of eternal blessing results in the eternal glorification of God. This is the ultimate purpose of the entire Protocol Plan of God for the Church Age believer.

IV. Point 11 — Undeserved Suffering as Impetus for the Third Hope

Undeserved suffering provides impetus and stimulation for the third hope, thus increasing the momentum of phase two. The classical formulation of this principle appears in Romans 5:2–5, where the sequence of pressure, endurance, approved character, and hope is traced with precision. The principle is stated proverbially in the Latin axiom:

semper ille malum non venit per nocere — misfortune does not always come to injure. What the believer receives as adversity is frequently designed by the justice of God for blessing. Undeserved suffering, received with doctrine resident in the soul and the third hope operational, becomes the highest plane of Christian experience available in time.

Romans 8:23–25 places the third hope in direct relationship with suffering: the believer groans inwardly, awaiting the redemption of the body, yet does so in hope — confident anticipation of what the justice of God has prepared. Romans 8:35–37 extends the same correlation: nothing in the created order is capable of separating the mature believer from the love of God, and in all these things the believer overwhelmingly conquers through Christ.

Romans 12:12 brings the two elements together in the command: 'With reference to the hope, be rejoicing; with reference to the pressures of undeserved suffering, stand fast.' This is the highest operational attainment of any believer in time — the capacity to face maximum adversity with maximum confidence, grounded in the third hope and the character of God.

V. Point 12 — The Third Hope as the Highest Motivation in the Christian Life

The third hope is the highest motivation available to the believer in time. It is the synthesis of everything the doctrine of hope has established: the character of God as the exclusive source of security and blessing, the two judicial imputations as the grace mechanism, doctrine as the indispensable means, undeserved suffering as the accelerant, and the judgment seat of Christ as the terminus and consummation. The mature believer who possesses the third hope as a structural element of his soul thinking is free from the compulsive anxiety over possessions, status, relationships, and outcomes that characterizes both the immature believer and the unbeliever.

The possession of the third hope purifies motivation in the sense of 1 John 3:3. The believer whose confidence is anchored in what God has prepared in eternity has no need to hoard, to coerce, or to maneuver in order to secure blessing in time. The blessings of time, when they come through the justice of God at and beyond the maturity barrier, are received with capacity, appreciated with occupation with Christ, and freed entirely from the anxiety that accompanies blessing received without capacity.

VI. Point 13 — The Function of Hope in Historical Disaster

The doctrine of hope has a thirteenth point concerning the function of hope in national and historical catastrophe. This point is acknowledged here as part of the complete structure of the doctrine but is not treated in the present chapter, as the expository sequence moves directly to Romans 15:5 and the doctrine of the mental attitude honor code. The function of hope in historical disaster will be treated when the expository context requires it.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Five

1. The second hope is structural, not sentimental. It is grounded in the judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation and the invariable principle that divine justice can only bless divine righteousness. Once the believer understands this, the second hope provides both absolute confidence about the future and operational motivation for daily doctrine intake.

2. Capacity determines the character of blessing. Divine blessing imputed without capacity produces misery rather than happiness. God's perfect wisdom and justice preclude the imputation of blessing beyond the believer's doctrinal capacity, not because God lacks resources, but because blessing without capacity defeats the purpose of glorifying God and produces the opposite of what was intended.

3. The double portion of divine righteousness in the Church Age increases both expectation and responsibility. Church Age believers receive imputed righteousness at salvation and shared righteousness through union with Christ via the baptism of the Holy Spirit. This double portion means that the grace pipeline from divine justice is correspondingly enlarged, and the potential for blessing is proportionally greater than in any previous dispensation.

4. The third hope governs the mature believer's relationship to undeserved suffering. When the third hope is resident in the soul as a structural system of thinking, undeserved suffering loses its power to destabilize. It becomes instead the impetus that accelerates advance, deepens capacity, and intensifies anticipation of the eternal blessing reserved at the judgment seat of Christ.

5. The omniscience of God eliminates every category of injustice at the judgment seat of Christ. Because God knows the counterfactual — what the positive believer would have attained had the rapture not intervened — no believer is disadvantaged by the timing of the rapture. The justice of God adjudicates at the judgment seat with perfect knowledge of both what occurred and what would have occurred.

6. Logistical grace is the foundation on which the second hope rests in daily experience. Lamentations 3:22–24 establishes that the Lord's gracious functions never cease and that His compassions are renewed every morning. The daily evidence of logistical grace — physical life, provision, doctrine available, a pastor to teach it — is itself the continuous confirmation that the justice of God is faithful and that the advance to maturity is both possible and guaranteed for the positive believer.

7. The third hope as anchor produces stability that no external circumstance can remove. Hebrews 6:19 describes the third hope as an anchor of the soul — secure and dependable — that reaches into the very presence of God where Christ has entered as forerunner. The stability this produces is not stoic indifference but the dynamic confidence of one who knows that the outcome is secured by divine integrity and that the path to that outcome is already guaranteed by the two judicial imputations.

Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Six

Romans 15:5 — Mental Attitude in the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 15:5 “May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Now may the God of perseverance and encouragement give to you to be thinking the same category of things, Bible doctrine, at your stage of growth, in the presence of one another according to Christ Jesus.

Romans 15 continues the exegesis of the Royal Family Honor Code. The preceding verses (15:1–4) established that mature believers are obligated to bear the weaknesses of the immature rather than accommodate themselves, and that the Old Testament scriptures were written for the instruction of the Church Age believer, so that through perseverance and encouragement from scripture we might have hope. Verse 5 now introduces the function of mental attitude as the operational center of the honor code.

I. Orienting the Verse: The Forgotten Priority of Thought

A foundational observation governs verse 5: many people have destroyed themselves through physical excess, but no one has ever thought himself to death. Thinking — specifically the thinking of Bible doctrine — is not anti-Christian. It is, in fact, the primary mechanism by which the plan of God is fulfilled in the life of the believer. Emotion, sincerity, activity, and social engagement are not substitutes for doctrinal thinking. The verse before us sets out a divine wish that the royal family of God function precisely at the level of disciplined, doctrine-saturated thought.

The verse opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle translated 'now,' marking a transition from the doctrinal basis established in verse 4 to its application in the believer's mental life.

II. The Subject: 'The God of Perseverance and Encouragement'

A. The Subject Noun

The subject is ho theos (ὁ θεός), 'the God' — the perfect, eternal God of scripture, infinite and personal, not a figure from mythology or an anthropomorphic projection. This is the God who has always existed and whose attributes are without deficiency or limit.

B. The Genitive Attributes: Perseverance and Encouragement

Modifying the subject are two descriptive genitive singular nouns. The first is hupomonē (ὑπομονή), translated 'perseverance' or 'endurance.' This noun appeared in verse 4 ('through perseverance and encouragement from the scriptures we might have hope') and is now reintroduced as an attribute of God himself. The second is paraklēsis (παράκλησις), 'encouragement' or 'comfort,' also carried forward from verse 4. The repetition is deliberate: these two qualities are the very substance of what makes life meaningful, and they are grounded not in human temperament but in God's own character.

Because perseverance and encouragement are presented as divine attributes applied to human experience, this phrase functions as an anthropopathism — an accommodation of the divine nature to human language in order to communicate how God operates within the framework of the Protocol Plan of God. The intent is practical: God, who is the very source of perseverance and encouragement, transmits these qualities to the believer through Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

C. The Principle of Perseverance in Doctrine

Perseverance as used here is not a vague general virtue. It refers specifically to the academic discipline of plodding through the intake of Bible doctrine with dogged, laborious determination — especially through material that does not immediately engage the believer's existing interests or present circumstances. Every subject in the canon is part of a unified structural system. The passages that seem least interesting or applicable are frequently foundational to the very doctrines that the believer finds most compelling. No portion of scripture was placed there for others but not for the individual believer. God makes no mistakes, and the assumption that certain portions of the Word are optional reveals the narrowness of personal selfishness or the limitation of personal ambition rather than any deficiency in the text itself.

Perseverance is the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). It means listening to and learning doctrine when one is tired, disinterested, occupied with personal problems, or drawn by the pull of a favorite subject. It means building the edification complex in the soul systematically, so that every part of the structure has its foundation.

The relevance of this perseverance becomes most acute at the point of maximum pressure — the moment of complete personal disaster, when physical energy is exhausted, emotional reserves are depleted, and human support has failed. At that moment, the only resource available is the thought that remains in the soul. If that thought is doctrinal, it functions as the exploitation force — the reserve unit committed at the breakthrough — sustaining forward motion when every other faculty has given out. One doctrinal thought, activated by the filling of the Holy Spirit, constitutes the supernatural energy that produces continued momentum and, from that momentum, either encouragement or comfort depending on the nature of the crisis.

Encouragement arises when doctrinal momentum is advancing and the believer begins to perceive the structural coherence of systematic theology. Comfort arises when the believer is in the midst of acute suffering and doctrine stabilizes the soul from within. Both are products of doctrine already resident in the soul — not of doctrine sought after the crisis has arrived.

III. The Verb: A Voluntative Optative

The main verb is the aorist active optative of didōmi (δίδωμι), 'to give,' rendered here 'may give.' The aorist is constative — it contemplates the action of the verb in its entirety, referring to action extended over a period of time. The active voice indicates that God produces the action, working through the medium of doctrine. The optative mood is the voluntative optative, expressing Paul's wish or strong desire for the future. The optative contains no guarantee of realization; it presents the action as conceivable and desired, not certain. This grammatical choice is significant: Paul cannot compel the Romans to persevere in doctrine. No teacher, no pastor, no mechanism of social pressure can substitute for the individual's own volitional decision to pursue the intake of Bible doctrine consistently.

The indirect object is the dative plural of the second-person personal pronoun — 'to you,' referring to all members of the royal family of God. This is a dative of advantage where positive volition toward doctrine exists, and a dative of disadvantage where negative volition prevails. The reversionist believer does not profit from this wish; the advantage belongs only to those who persevere.

IV. The Infinitive: 'To Be Thinking the Same Category of Things'

The object of the verb is the present active infinitive of phroneō (φρονέω), with the accusative neuter plural of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός). The full phrase is to auto phronein — 'to be thinking the same things,' or more precisely, 'to be thinking the same category of things.'

The verb phroneō means to think, to form a thought, to hold an opinion, to set the mind on specific content, to sculpt one's mental life around particular categories. It is not passive cognition but active, deliberate mental engagement. The present tense is a customary present, denoting what habitually occurs among believers who persevere in the perception of Bible doctrine.

The intensive pronoun emphasizes identity — the 'same things' in question are not a uniformity of doctrinal maturity or an identical knowledge base across all members of the royal family, since believers are at vastly different stages of growth. The 'same category' is Bible doctrine and the divine viewpoint it produces. What is shared is not an identical inventory of knowledge but the same orientation: the mind set on the thinking of Christ (cf. 1 Corinthians 2:16).

The infinitive is an infinitive of intended result, blending purpose and result into a single concept. The result indicated fulfills a deliberate aim: that believers, through perseverance in doctrine, would come to share a common doctrinal orientation that governs their mental life.

V. The Prepositional Phrase: 'In the Presence of One Another'

The phrase is en allēlois (ἐν ἀλλήλοις) — the preposition en plus the dative plural of the reciprocal pronoun allēlōn (ἀλλήλων). The reciprocal pronoun in the plural signifies an interchange of action — what goes on between persons in contact. The dative of presence yields the translation 'in the presence of one another.'

Human interaction is the inevitable context in which mental attitude functions. The question raised by this phrase is whether the believer, in the presence of others, is capable of thinking in terms of divine viewpoint: evaluating accurately, perceiving the needs and circumstances of others, exercising the mental sensitivity that only doctrine produces. Awareness of another person's failures is easy and natural; awareness of their need for thoughtful regard requires doctrine resident in the soul.

The principle follows directly: reciprocity between believers must be based on thinking doctrine. Without doctrinal content in the soul, human interaction defaults to the categories of the old sin nature — judgment, jealousy, self-promotion, or sentimental attachment mistaken for love.

VI. The Final Phrase: 'According to Christ Jesus'

The verse closes with the prepositional phrase kata Christon Iēsoun (κατὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν), 'according to Christ Jesus.' The preposition kata with the accusative establishes the standard of conformity. The standard by which doctrinal thinking in the presence of others is to be measured is Christ Jesus himself — his mind, his character, his thinking as revealed in scripture (1 Corinthians 2:16).

This phrase anchors the entire verse theologically. Mental attitude in the Royal Family Honor Code is not merely a psychological discipline or a social technique. It is participation in the thinking of the Lord Jesus Christ, made possible by the indwelling Holy Spirit and the doctrine stored in the soul through sustained perseverance in the perception of scripture.

VII. The Corrected Translation of Romans 15:5

Now may the God of perseverance and encouragement give to you to be thinking the same category of things — Bible doctrine, at your stage of growth — in the presence of one another according to Christ Jesus.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Six

1. The God of perseverance and encouragement transmits these attributes to believers through Bible doctrine. God does not communicate perseverance and encouragement through emotion, religious activity, or social support structures. The channel is doctrine received, stored, and activated in the soul.

2. Perseverance is the single virtue required for doctrinal perception. It is the willingness to learn doctrine systematically — including subjects that hold no immediate interest or apparent relevance — because the entire structure of the edification complex depends on all its components, not merely those the believer finds personally engaging.

3. The anthropopathism 'God of perseverance and encouragement' establishes royal family guidelines. The phrase accommodates divine policy to human language in order to communicate what God expects of the royal family: perseverance in the intake of doctrine so that encouragement and comfort are available from within the soul when needed.

4. No one can be coerced into perseverance in doctrine. The voluntative optative in which Paul frames this verse reflects the limits of even apostolic authority. Paul can teach; he cannot compel. The decision to persevere belongs entirely to the individual believer's volition.

5. Bible doctrine is the only resource that does not fail at the point of maximum pressure. When physical energy is gone, emotional reserves are exhausted, and human support has disappeared, the only resource remaining is the thought in the soul. If that thought is doctrinal, it constitutes the supernatural force that sustains momentum through and beyond the crisis.

6. God is the God of perseverance and encouragement. Since these are divine attributes, God expects believers to reflect them through daily, consistent function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Perseverance in learning doctrine is the means; encouragement and comfort are the results produced once doctrine is resident in the soul.

7. Encouragement is the result of perseverance in doctrinal perception. When the believer is advancing in momentum, the structural coherence of systematic theology produces encouragement. When the believer is under pressure, the same resident doctrine produces comfort. Both outcomes require that doctrine already be in the soul before the occasion for its use arises.

8. The verb phroneō denotes active, deliberate, sculpted thought. The present tense marks this as the habitual characteristic of believers who persevere in doctrine. It is not passive reception of information but the active shaping of the mind around the content of scripture — the mind of Christ.

9. The 'same category of things' is Bible doctrine and the divine viewpoint it produces. Uniformity of doctrinal knowledge across all believers at different stages of growth is not in view. What is shared is a common orientation: the mind set on scripture as the framework for evaluating all of life.

10. Reciprocity between believers must be based on thinking doctrine. The dative of the reciprocal pronoun places doctrinal thinking in the context of human interaction. The quality of one believer's regard for another is a direct function of the doctrine resident in the soul — specifically, the inflexibility regarding essentials and flexibility regarding non-essentials that only mature doctrinal thinking produces.

11. Thinking doctrine is not anti-Christian. It is the motivation, the momentum, and the fulfillment of the plan of God. The substitution of emotion, sincerity, or social engagement for doctrinal thought produces a soul that is perpetually seeking external stimulation because it has no internal resources.

12. The standard for all doctrinal thinking in the presence of others is Christ Jesus himself. The phrase kata Christon Iēsoun closes the verse by anchoring mental attitude in the Royal Family Honor Code to the person and thinking of the Lord, as revealed in scripture and made accessible by the indwelling Holy Spirit.

Perseverance in Romans 15:5 refers directly to the daily, consistent function of GAP.
Royal Family Honor Code The system of norms and standards governing the conduct of Church Age believers as members of the royal family of God. Romans 15 applies this code specifically to the relationship between strong (mature) and weak (immature) believers, with mental attitude — doctrinal thinking — as its operational center.

Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Seven

Romans 15:5–6 — Unanimity, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Glorification of God

Romans 15:5–6 “May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus, that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Now may the God of perseverance and encouragement give to you to be thinking the same category of things — that is, Bible doctrine and resultant divine viewpoint — in the presence of one another according to Christ Jesus, in order that with one motivation, doctrine resident in the soul, by one message, doctrinal teaching from one's right pastor, you may glorify the God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The exegesis of Romans 15:5 was completed in the previous chapter. The present chapter extracts the doctrinal principles embedded in that verse and then moves into the exegesis of verse 6, where Paul states the governing objective of the Royal Family Honor Code: the glorification of God through the teaching and perception of Bible doctrine. The two verses form a single unit — verse 5 identifies the means, verse 6 identifies the end.

I. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 15:5 — Unanimity and the Honor Code

Point 1: Unanimity Requires Something with Which to Think

Verse 5 requires unanimity among believers — but unanimity is impossible apart from a common basis for thinking. That basis is Bible doctrine. Believers at every stage of spiritual growth carry different norms and standards. The new believer has little doctrine and a great deal of residual human viewpoint. The adolescent believer has accumulated more doctrine and his standards have begun to shift accordingly. The believer approaching the maturity barrier has sufficient doctrine to handle undeserved suffering and to persevere through the testing that cracks that barrier. The mature believer — having passed through supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace — looks back across that entire spectrum with complete tolerance, understanding that no two believers have reached exactly the same stage of spiritual growth.

Unanimity, therefore, does not mean doctrinal uniformity at every point. It means that doctrine is the common issue at every stage. The mature believer does not intrude upon the privacy of the growing believer, does not malign or ridicule erroneous standards, and does not attempt to accelerate growth by external pressure. He tolerates, he perseveres, and he models the very flexibility that the honor code demands — inflexible on the essentials of doctrine, fully flexible on the non-essentials.

Point 2: Doctrinal Perception Operates at Different Levels

Even among believers who are positive toward doctrine, perception is at different levels, producing different stages of spiritual growth. The critical distinction is not between those who agree on every point but between those who are positive toward doctrine and those who are in reversionism. The reversionistic believer — negative toward doctrine — is headed toward warning discipline, intensive discipline, and ultimately the sin unto death. Toward that believer, the application of the honor code is separation, a subject taken up in the following chapter. Toward the believer who is positive toward doctrine, however — whatever his stage — the application is toleration, impersonal love, and respect for the privacy of the priesthood.

Point 3: The Honor Code Provides Freedom for Spiritual Advance

The Royal Family Honor Code governs the relationships among believers in the local church precisely so that doctrine can remain the issue for each individual. The honor code functions through impersonal love — love that emphasizes the subject rather than the object and that is sustained by norms and standards developed from Bible doctrine. Impersonal love respects privacy, protects property, and preserves the freedom of every believer to concentrate on doctrine without distraction.

The three categories of love operative in the Christian life are: (1) personal love for the Lord Jesus Christ — occupation with Christ, the mark of the mature believer; (2) personal love for right man or right woman; and (3) personal love for friends, family, and loved ones. When the New Testament commands loving the brethren or loving one's neighbor, it is not commanding personal love but impersonal love — a mental attitude grounded in doctrine that functions irrespective of the object. Impersonal love is what the honor code demands, and it is the only form of love adequate to sustain toleration across all the differences of spiritual growth within a congregation.

Point 4: The Honor Code Serves Each Stage of Growth

God has provided through the honor code something applicable to every stage of spiritual life. For the weak believer who is positive toward doctrine, the operative principle is the privacy of the priesthood — a prohibition against judging and maligning believers who have advanced beyond him. For the strong believer, the operative principle is impersonal love and the resultant flexibility and toleration in the non-essentials of life. The honor code does not require equal doctrine among believers; it requires equal respect for each believer's freedom to pursue doctrine.

Point 5: Believers Cannot Think Alike but Can Think in Terms of the Honor Code

Because of the different stages of growth represented in any congregation, believers cannot think identically. A new believer, an adolescent believer, a believer approaching the maturity barrier, and a mature believer will evaluate circumstances differently. What they share is the obligation of the honor code — the duty to give privacy, to respect property, and to preserve freedom so that doctrine is always the issue at every stage. This common obligation is the one thing that can hold a diverse congregation together and allow momentum to be sustained across the full spectrum of spiritual growth.

Point 6: Allegiance to Christ Obligates to the Honor Code

Allegiance to the Lord Jesus Christ — the meaning of the phrase 'according to Christ Jesus' in verse 5 — obligates every believer to the Royal Family Honor Code. This allegiance demands that the rights of every believer priest be respected: privacy in the local church, in social life, and in business life. The practices specifically prohibited by the honor code — judging, maligning, gossip, ridicule, retaliation, revenge, implacability, and arrogance — are prohibited precisely because each one distracts from doctrine and destroys the freedom necessary for spiritual advance.

Point 7: No Believer Is an Isolated Ambassador

No believer is authorized to think of himself as functioning in isolation. Every believer is a member of the Royal priesthood and a Royal ambassador. The function of the Royal priesthood — taking in doctrine and advancing to maturity — is the subject of this passage. The function of ambassadorship — Christian production — is the consequence of that growth. As part of a corporate royal priesthood, every believer is obligated to impersonal love, thoughtfulness, and sensitivity to the stage of growth in which other members of the priesthood are found.

Point 8: Every Believer Has Royal Priesthood Status

There is no believer who stands above or below the royal priesthood. Every member of the royal family of God has privacy, has the breathing room to live his life as unto the Lord, and has the right to gain momentum from his thinking without external interference. The honor code protects that status for every believer equally.

Point 9: No Believer Receives Preferred Treatment

No believer is a star with preferred treatment. Every believer is a member of the team, subject to team policy and team discipline. The Royal Family Honor Code admits no special cases. The principle of the privacy of the priesthood applies uniformly, from the newest believer to the most advanced.

Point 10: Believers Must Think in Terms of Others

The believer must learn to think in terms of others rather than solely in terms of himself. This means recognizing that other believers have feelings, that they are at different stages of spiritual growth, and that differences in appearance, conduct, and cultural expression are not the believer's business to correct. The privacy of the priesthood extends to every dimension of a fellow believer's life. The sole exception is the pastor, whose authority over the local church must itself be exercised with careful restraint so that every individual retains the same opportunity to hear the Word of God. Doctrine is always the issue. The objective of thinking in terms of others is not social conformity but the creation of the conditions under which every believer can concentrate on doctrine without distraction or deterrence.

II. Exegesis of Romans 15:6

The Purpose Clause: Hina

Verse 6 opens with the Greek conjunction ἵνα (hina), which together with the subjunctive mood of the following verb introduces a purpose clause. The entire verse states the objective toward which the principle of verse 5 is directed. Translated: in order that.

Homothymadon — With One Motivation

The next word is the adverb ὁμοθυμαδόν (homothymadon), a compound of the adverb ὁμο- (homo-, meaning together or in the same place) and θυμός (thymos, the mind or soul under strong passion — anger, rage, or simply intense motivation). The compound adverb conveys the inner unity of a group engaged in similar action. Aristophanes used it for the political decision of a corporate body. In the New Testament it denotes the inner unanimity of the royal family of God, but in this context it specifically denotes motivation arising from doctrine resident in the soul. Corrected translation: with one motivation. The one motivation is doctrine — for doctrine is the ammunition with which the believer thinks, the substance that awakens divine viewpoint and drives the dynamics of the Christian way of life.

En Stomati — By One Message

The prepositional phrase that follows is ἐν (en) plus the instrumental singular of στόμα (stoma, mouth). In classical Greek, from Aeschylus, Euripides, and Demosthenes onward, the word for mouth was regularly used as a synonym for a speaker or for what is said, rather than for the physical organ of speech. In Matthew 4:4, Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3 — 'Man shall not live by bread alone but by every word which proceeds out of the mouth of God' — where stoma functions as an anthropomorphism for the message of God, for Bible doctrine itself. In Romans 15:6 the phrase therefore does not mean 'with one physical mouth' but by one message. That one message is doctrinal teaching — the consistent systematic teaching of Bible doctrine by one's right pastor. Corrected translation of the phrase: by one message, doctrinal teaching from one's right pastor.

Doxasēte — You May Glorify

The main verb of the purpose clause is the present active subjunctive of δοξάζω (doxazō, to glorify). The present tense is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results. The existing results are the daily advance toward maturity produced by the consistent function of GAP — the Grace Apparatus for Perception — under the ministry of God the Holy Spirit. As doctrine is taken in today and tomorrow and the day after, the cumulative result is advance toward the maturity adjustment to the justice of God, and through that advance, the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ. The active voice indicates that the mature believer produces this action by persisting in his positive volition toward doctrine. The subjunctive mood combined with hina marks this as a purpose clause with potential force: the potential is realized through continued doctrinal intake.

Ton Theon — The God

The accusative singular direct object is τὸν θεόν (ton theon). The definite article indicates previous reference — this is the God already under discussion. The specific member of the Trinity is identified by what follows.

Kai Patera — Even the Father

The conjunction καί (kai) here carries the ascensive force: even. The following accusative singular πατέρα (patera, Father) stands in apposition to theon: God, even the Father. This identifies the first person of the Trinity as the one glorified — the Father who sent the Son and who is the ultimate recipient of the glorification that flows from the believer's doctrinal advance.

Tou Kyriou Hēmōn Iēsou Christou — Of Our Lord Jesus Christ

The genitive chain that closes the verse contains three terms, each carrying a distinct theological weight. κύριος (kyrios, Lord) designates the eternal deity of Christ — he possesses all the attributes of the Godhead. Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous, Jesus) designates his true humanity — essential for the cross, for it was as the Last Adam, as a true human being, that he could be judged for human sins, die physically, and rise in a resurrection body. Χριστός (Christos, Christ) designates his appointment to battlefield royalty. In the ancient world, anointing with oil was the mechanism of commissioning; Christos means the Anointed One, the Commissioned One — appointed to his royal role as the strategic victor in the angelic conflict. The hypostatic union — full deity and true humanity combined in one person — underlies each of these terms and makes the entire plan of salvation coherent.

The full corrected translation of verse 6 is therefore: In order that with one motivation — doctrine resident in the soul — by one message — doctrinal teaching from one's right pastor — you may glorify the God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

III. The Objective of the Honor Code: Glorification of God

Verse 6 functions as the stated purpose of the entire preceding context. God never gives a policy for the royal family without also providing its purpose and objective somewhere in the context. The objective articulated in verse 6 is the glorification of God through the teaching and perception of Bible doctrine. Every structural element of the honor code is designed to protect that objective.

Glorification of God in the believer's experience is not produced by witnessing, by Christian service, by prayer, by moral conduct, by the observation of cultural taboos, or by any form of external religious activity. All of those activities, many of which are legitimate, are the consequence and manifestation of spiritual growth — not its cause. They are motivated by doctrine under the filling of the Spirit; they are not the mechanism of advance. The only mechanism of advance is the consistent intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception under the ministry of God the Holy Spirit. Doctrine is the means; glorification of God is the end.

The principle of one message — doctrinal teaching from one's right pastor — points to the importance of systematic verse-by-verse teaching as the vehicle of doctrinal perception. The emphasis on one motivation — doctrine resident in the soul — points to the interior condition required: doctrine must be not merely heard but retained in the right lobe, available for thinking, for the application of divine viewpoint to circumstances, and for the accumulation of momentum toward the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Seven

1. Glorification of God can only be accomplished through the teaching and perception of Bible doctrine. Witnessing, prayer, moral conduct, church service, and all forms of Christian production are the consequence of doctrinal advance, not its cause. None of these activities, however legitimate, produces spiritual growth or the glorification of God in time.

2. The unanimity required by verse 5 is not uniformity of opinion but unity of motivation. The common motivation is doctrine. Believers at every stage of growth share the obligation to make doctrine the issue and to respect the honor code that protects doctrinal intake for every other believer.

3. The Royal Family Honor Code has something specific for each stage of spiritual growth. For the weak believer who is positive toward doctrine, the operative principle is the privacy of the priesthood — a prohibition against judging and maligning believers who have advanced beyond him. For the strong believer, the operative principle is impersonal love and the resultant flexibility and toleration in the non-essentials of life.

4. Impersonal love is the form of love commanded when the New Testament commands loving the brethren. Impersonal love emphasizes the subject — the one producing the action — and is sustained by norms and standards developed from Bible doctrine. It functions irrespective of the object and is therefore adequate to sustain toleration across the full spectrum of differences in spiritual maturity within a congregation.

5. The honor code provides the breathing space necessary for every believer to advance to maturity. Without the honor code, believers divide into areas of bickering, retaliation, revenge, and implacable criticism, and doctrine ceases to be the issue. The honor code suppresses these distractions so that every believer can concentrate on the intake of doctrine.

6. Allegiance to Christ Jesus obligates every believer to the Royal Family Honor Code. This allegiance demands respect for the rights of every believer priest in the local church, in social life, and in business life — privacy, property, and the freedom to take in doctrine without interference.

7. No believer functions as an isolated individual. Every believer is a member of the Royal priesthood and a Royal ambassador. As part of a corporate royal priesthood, every believer is obligated to impersonal love, thoughtfulness, and sensitivity to the stage of growth in which other members of the priesthood are found.

8. No believer receives preferred treatment under the honor code. Every believer is a member of the team, subject to team policy and team discipline. The privacy of the priesthood applies uniformly across every stage of spiritual growth.

9. The objective of the honor code is to advance every believer to the maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Through that maturity, God's plan is fulfilled with the sixth imputation — blessing in time — and the believer moves toward the absolute confidence of the seventh imputation at the judgment seat of Christ: eternal blessing in resurrection.

10. The homothymadon of verse 6 — one motivation — is doctrine resident in the soul. The en stomati of verse 6 — one message — is systematic doctrinal teaching from one's right pastor. Together these two elements constitute the mechanism by which believers glorify the God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
