Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
leitourgos λειτουργός leitourgos — minister, servant, one who performs public or sacrificial service Noun used in the LXX for Levitical priests (Hebrews 8:2) and in broader Greek usage for government officials and public servants. In Romans 15:16 Paul applies it to himself as apostolic communicator of doctrine to the Gentiles, combining the senses of servant, official, priestly minister, and altar-sacrifice functionary.
eis to with infinitive εἰς τό + infinitive eis to — purpose / result construction A Greek grammatical construction using the preposition eis plus the accusative definite article to followed by an infinitive, introducing a purpose clause. May express deliberate design, general direction, or contemplated result; grammarians classify it as a final clause blending purpose and result.
presbuteros πρεσβύτερος presbuteros — elder, commanding officer One of five New Testament terms for the pastor-teacher. Literally 'old man,' used as a title of authority analogous to the military designation 'commanding officer.' One presbuteros per congregation; the concept of a rotating plurality of elders sharing the teaching function is without New Testament warrant.
poimenas ποιμένας poimenas — shepherd, pastor Accusative plural of poimen, shepherd. Used in Ephesians 4:11 in combination with didaskalos (teacher) to designate the pastor-teacher gift. Connotes both authority over and provision for the congregation as students under doctrinal instruction.
episkopos ἐπίσκοπος episkopos — overseer, guardian Compound: epi (over) + skopeo (to look, examine). Designates the administrative and policy-making dimension of the pastor-teacher's role — the guardian of the doctrinal system of the local church. Source of the English word 'episcopal.'
diakonos διάκονος diakonos — servant, deacon Originally a table waiter; extended to designate anyone functioning in a serving capacity. As applied to the pastor-teacher, it emphasizes the servant dimension of the communicator's role — serving spiritual food to the congregation.
didaskalos διδάσκαλος didaskalos — teacher The standard Greek word for teacher. Paired with poimenas in Ephesians 4:11 to form the compound gift designation pastor-teacher, indicating that the shepherd function and the teaching function are inseparable in this gift.
nabi נָבִיא nabi — prophet, spokesman Hebrew noun for prophet. Designates the official communicator of doctrine in the dispensation of Israel. Two sub-categories: those holding the office of prophet (full-time communicators) and those holding only the gift of prophecy (who also fulfilled other roles). First clearly instantiated in Moses.
einai εἶναι einai — to be (present active infinitive) Present active infinitive of eimi, the verb of being. In Romans 15:16 it serves as the infinitive of intended result in the eis to construction. The present tense here is a historical present, viewing Paul's past appointment with vividness.
ethnos ἔθνος ethnos — nation, Gentile Noun used in the singular for a nation or people-group, and in the plural (ethne) for the Gentiles as distinguished from Israel. In Romans 15:16 Paul's commission eis ta ethne — to the Gentiles — defines the scope of his apostolic leitourgos ministry.
Logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and ministry function. In Romans 15:15–16 the grace given to Paul (verse 15) is the logistical and gift-based support for his apostolic ministry as leitourgos (verse 16). Logistical grace is coextensive with God's intended purpose for each believer.
GAP — Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which the believer receives, perceives, and internalizes Bible doctrine under the ministry of God the Holy Spirit. Operates through consistent attendance under the right pastor-teacher. Required for advancement from spiritual infancy through the maturity barrier to supergrace and ultra-supergrace.
Maturity barrier The threshold of spiritual maturity that is cracked through sustained and consistent doctrine intake under the GAP. Defined in Ephesians 4:13 as attaining the full knowledge of the Son of God to the standard of the fullness of Christ. Cannot be crossed by irregular or eclectic exposure to teaching.

Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven

Romans 15:16 — Priestly Ministry and the Communication of Doctrine

Romans 15:15b–16 “…because of the grace given me by God to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: …because of the grace which has been given to me from God, that I should be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, ministering as a priest the good news of God, in order that the offering consisting of the Gentiles might be acceptable, having been sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

Romans 15 continues Paul's extended personal statement begun in verse 15, where he defends the audacity of his letter by appealing to the grace commission entrusted to him. Having established that he is a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, the text moves deeper into the character of that ministry. Verse 16 introduces a Greek participle that reframes the entire discussion: Paul does not merely preach — he officiates as a priest, presenting the Gentiles themselves as a living offering to God. This chapter examines the meaning of that priestly service, its relationship to the communication of doctrine, and its application to any believer equipped and motivated to teach.

I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest

The key word in verse 16 is the present active participle translated 'ministering' in most English versions. The Greek term is

hierourgounta (ἱερουργοῦντα), the present active participle of the verb hierourgeō (ἱερουργέω), a compound of hieros (ἱερός, sacred, holy) and ergazomai (ἐργάζομαι, to work, to perform). The compound means to perform sacred rites — specifically the ritual functions of a priest at the altar.

The present tense is progressive: the priestly action is continuous, linear, and sustained. Paul is not describing a single act of proclamation but an ongoing mode of ministry. The participle modifies his role as a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles and specifies the manner in which that ministry is executed.

In the Levitical system, the priest did not merely speak — he acted visibly before the congregation. He placed the animal on the altar, explained its significance, transferred the worshiper's sins symbolically through the laying on of hands, and executed the sacrifice. Every step was a training aid. The blood, the fire, the aroma, the grain — all of it communicated doctrine in a form the observer could see, smell, and remember. The priest also renewed the table of showbread, tended the menorah, and maintained every article of the tabernacle and later the temple — each item a visual embodiment of a doctrinal reality.

Paul's use of this participle signals that his ministry among the Gentiles had this same character. He did not restrict himself to verbal exposition alone. He took the Levitical institutions — the burnt offering, the food offering, the peace offering, the sin offering, the trespass offering — and laid them open before Gentile audiences who had never encountered Judaism. By means of these inherited training aids, he made propitiation, reconciliation, the person of Christ, and the rebound principle concrete and memorable.

II. The Direct Object: The Gospel of God

The phrase translated 'the gospel of God' consists of the possessive genitive singular of theos (θεός, God) governing the accusative singular direct object euangelion (εὐαγγέλιον). In its general, non-technical sense euangelion means simply good news. In its technical and restricted sense it refers to the gospel of salvation — faith in Christ as the sole basis of justification before God. Both meanings are in view here. Paul ministers the specific saving message, but the vehicle of that ministry is the entire wealth of revealed doctrine, the full good news of God's redemptive plan as disclosed through the Old Testament institutions and fulfilled in Christ.

Similarly, the word apostle (

apostolos, ἀπόστολος) carries both a technical and a general sense. In its technical sense it refers to the unique office held by the Twelve (with Judas replaced) and by Paul — individuals directly commissioned by the risen Christ and bearing foundational authority for the Church Age. In its general sense it can describe a missionary, one sent out with a specific message. Paul operates under the technical sense here, but the ministry he describes — priestly communication of the good news — extends beyond that office to any qualified, motivated believer.

III. The Purpose Clause: The Offering of the Gentiles

The conjunction introducing the purpose clause is

hina (ἵνα), which governs a semi-final clause expressing the aim and anticipated result of the priestly ministry. The subject of the purpose clause is the nominative singular prosphora (προσφορά), meaning the act of bringing or presenting an offering. The offering in view is the Gentiles themselves — not an offering made by the Gentiles but an offering consisting of the Gentiles, expressed by the appositional genitive plural of ethnos (ἔθνος, nation, Gentile people).

Paul casts his entire Gentile ministry in sacrificial terms. Every Gentile believer brought to faith and grounded in doctrine is, in Paul's imagery, a living sacrifice presented to God. The priest's labor — sustained, visual, explanatory — produces an offering. The offering is the congregation he has built. The completion of this purpose clause (that the offering might be acceptable, having been sanctified by the Holy Spirit) will be taken up in the following section of verse 16; the present chapter focuses on the nature of the priestly function itself.

What made the Gentiles a striking offering was precisely their distance from Israel's heritage. They had no prior exposure to the tabernacle, the priesthood, the Levitical calendar, or the sacrificial system. When Paul introduced these things, the effect was immediate and powerful. The Galatians, for example, responded with the enthusiasm of children encountering something entirely new. Their lack of familiarity was not an obstacle to understanding; it was the condition for fresh wonder. The training aids of Israel, explained by a skilled priest-communicator to audiences who had never seen them, produced exactly the kind of doctrinal retention for which those aids had been designed.

IV. Prophet and Priest — Two Modes of Communication

The Old Testament distinguished the prophet from the priest along functional lines that remain instructive for the Church Age. The prophet was the verbal communicator par excellence: he stood before the people and declared the word of God with direct propositional force. The priest was the visual communicator: he performed, demonstrated, and enacted the realities the prophet declared. Both functions were necessary, and neither was superior to the other.

In the Church Age, the gift of pastor-teacher corresponds to the prophetic mode: the male believer with this gift is responsible for the authoritative, systematic exposition of Scripture to the assembled congregation. The priestly mode, however, belongs to the entire royal family of God. Every Church Age believer is a priest — a member of the royal priesthood — and therefore every believer who has acquired sufficient doctrine and is motivated by that doctrine may function as a priest-communicator in the appropriate context.

This distinction has direct bearing on the question of who may teach doctrine to children. The pastor-teacher's gift is not in view when a believer uses visual materials, flannel boards, object lessons, or other training aids to communicate doctrinal realities to young learners. That is priestly function, open to men and women alike, requiring doctrine, motivation, and the absence of spiritual arrogance but not the specific gift of pastor-teacher.

V. Training Aids and the Principle of Doctrinal Retention

The Levitical system was the ancient world's most sophisticated curriculum. Its genius lay in the fact that it did not require its students to be literate. A worshiper who watched the burnt offering year after year could not avoid learning propitiation. A family that observed the peace offering understood reconciliation experientially before they could articulate it theologically. The training aids did not replace verbal instruction; they embedded it at a level deeper than cognition alone could reach.

This principle governs effective communication of doctrine in any dispensation. When the priest-communicator introduces a visual element — an object, a demonstration, a model, a map, a living illustration — the student's attention engages at a different level than it does during purely verbal instruction. The visual element creates a frame of reference to which subsequent verbal teaching can be attached. The doctrine then travels with the image and is recalled when the image is recalled.

Flexibility in the choice of training aids is not a concession to intellectual weakness but a mark of skilled priestly ministry. The Levitical system itself employed a range of media: fire, blood, grain, oil, incense, woven fabric, hammered gold, acacia wood, linen, animal skins. No two offerings were identical in their materials or their emphasis. This variety was deliberate. Different sensory and conceptual registers were engaged by different offerings, ensuring that no single doctrinal truth was taught through only one medium. The priest who understood this variety did not insist on a single approved method; he selected from the full range of available aids the one most suited to his audience and occasion.

Effective priestly communication also requires the absence of arrogance — on two counts. First, the priest-communicator must not be so attached to a particular method that he refuses to adopt one better suited to his students. Second, he must not be so self-conscious about appearing undignified that he withholds aids his students need. Children in particular require the priest-communicator to meet them where they are, not where the communicator is comfortable.

VI. The Levitical Offerings as Doctrinal Training Aids

The Burnt Offering and Propitiation

The burnt offering (

olah, עֹלָה) was wholly consumed on the altar — nothing was retained by the offerer or the priest. The entire animal ascended as a pleasing aroma to God. This total consumption illustrated the substitutionary character of Christ's work: his humanity was fully offered to the justice of God in judgment for human sin. Propitiation is satisfied justice — the justice of God fully met by the penalty paid in the humanity of Christ. The burnt offering made this abstract truth visible and sensory.

The Food Offering and the Person of Christ

The food or grain offering (

minchah, מִנְחָה) illustrated the person of Christ in the hypostatic union. Fine flour without leaven (a type of sin) represented the sinless humanity of Christ. Oil pressed into the flour represented the indwelling Spirit. Salt, which preserves and prevents corruption, represented the incorruptibility of the divine nature. The priest-communicator who explained these details to Gentile audiences was making Christology concrete.

The Peace Offering and Reconciliation

The peace offering (

shelamim, שְׁלָמִים) was the only offering in which the offerer ate a portion. God received his portion on the altar; the priest received his portion; the offerer and his household ate their portion. This shared meal across the altar depicted reconciliation — the removal of enmity and the restoration of fellowship between the offerer and God. Paul's exposition of reconciliation in Romans 5 is grounded in exactly this imagery.

The Sin Offering and Unknown Sins

The sin offering (

chattat, חַטָּאת) addressed unintentional sins — violations committed without awareness. It illustrated the provision for unknown sins that require divine handling, corresponding in Church Age terms to the rebound principle: naming known sins to God under the mechanism of 1 John 1:9, with the understanding that unknown sins are handled by Christ's advocacy before the Father. The priest's role in the sin offering made this provision visible.

The Trespass Offering and Rebound

The trespass offering (

asham, אָשָׁם) addressed specific, known transgressions against God or man, with a requirement of restitution where applicable. It illustrated the rebound principle in its full scope: acknowledgment of the specific sin, reliance on the atoning work of Christ as the basis of forgiveness, and restoration to fellowship with God. The trespass offering made rebound not merely a concept but a procedure the worshiper enacted with his own hands.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven

1. The participle hierourgounta governs the entire description of Paul's ministry: he ministers as a priest, not merely as a herald. The distinction is functional — the priest communicates doctrine through enacted and visible means, not verbal proclamation alone. This characterizes the mode of ministry Paul claims for himself in his Gentile mission.

2. The present progressive tense of hierourgounta signals sustained, linear action: priestly ministry is not occasional but continuous. The priest-communicator does not offer a single dramatic presentation and withdraw; he maintains the discipline of consistent, sequential instruction using the full range of available aids.

3. The direct object euangelion carries both technical and general force: the specific saving message and the entire body of doctrinal good news. Paul ministers the gospel of salvation, but the vehicle is the comprehensive revelation of God — the Levitical institutions, the prophetic writings, and their fulfillment in the person and work of Christ.

4. The Levitical offerings were Israel's divinely designed curriculum: each offering taught a distinct doctrinal truth through a distinct sensory and procedural experience. The burnt offering illustrated propitiation; the food offering illustrated the person of Christ in hypostatic union; the peace offering illustrated reconciliation; the sin offering illustrated provision for unknown sins; the trespass offering illustrated rebound. Paul used these as training aids with Gentile audiences.

5. The offering consisting of the Gentiles (prosphora tōn ethnōn) is Paul's characterization of his entire Gentile mission: every believer brought to faith and maturity through priestly instruction constitutes a living sacrifice presented to God. The priest-communicator's labor produces the offering. The offering is the congregation.

6. The distinction between prophet and priest maps onto two distinct modes of communication in the Church Age: the gift of pastor-teacher corresponds to the prophetic mode and is restricted to the male believer with that gift. The priestly mode belongs to every member of the royal family of God and is exercised by any believer — male or female — who possesses sufficient doctrine and the motivation to communicate it using training aids appropriate to the audience.

7. Flexibility in method is not accommodation but fidelity to the priestly model: the Levitical system itself employed a wide range of materials, procedures, and sensory registers precisely because different doctrinal truths require different vehicles. The priest-communicator who insists on a single approved method impoverishes both the content and the reception of the doctrine he teaches.

8. Doctrinal retention is maximized when verbal instruction is accompanied by visual and procedural elements: the Levitical worshiper who enacted the trespass offering internalized rebound at a level that verbal description alone could not produce. This principle governs any effective communication of doctrine across any dispensation.

9. Effective priestly ministry requires the absence of arrogance in two forms: attachment to a preferred method that prevents adoption of a better one, and self-consciousness about appearing undignified that withholds aids the student needs. Neither the method nor the communicator's comfort is the standard — the doctrinal formation of the student is the standard.

10. The purpose clause (hina … prosphora … genētai euprosdektos) frames the entire ministry in terms of its eschatological goal: that the offering consisting of the Gentiles might be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. The priest-communicator works toward an outcome that only the Spirit can complete. The human instrument provides the sustained, flexible, doctrinally grounded instruction; the Spirit produces the acceptability of the offering before God.

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
hierourgeō ἱερουργέω hierourgeō — to perform sacred rites, to minister as a priest Compound verb: hieros (sacred) + ergazomai (to work, to perform). Denotes the execution of priestly duties at the altar, including sacrifice, ritual maintenance of sacred furnishings, and all visual-instructional functions of the Levitical priesthood. Used in Romans 15:16 to characterize Paul's mode of ministry among the Gentiles.
euangelion εὐαγγέλιον euangelion — good news, gospel In its technical sense, the saving message of faith in Christ as the sole basis of justification. In its general sense, the full body of divine revelation — all of the good news of God's redemptive plan. Both senses are operative in Romans 15:16.
prosphora προσφορά prosphora — offering, the act of presenting Noun from prospherō (to bring to, to present). Denotes the act of bringing an offering to God. In Romans 15:16, the offering consists of the Gentiles themselves — Gentile believers presented to God as a living sacrifice through Paul's priestly ministry.
ethnos ἔθνος ethnos — nation, Gentile people Refers to non-Jewish peoples, the Gentile nations. In the appositional genitive construction of Romans 15:16, the Gentiles are identified as the content of the offering — not the ones making the offering but the ones who constitute it.
apostolos ἀπόστολος apostolos — one sent, apostle Technical sense: one of the twelve foundational apostles of the Church Age, directly commissioned by the risen Christ; includes Paul as the apostle to the Gentiles. General sense: a missionary, one sent out with a specific message. The technical office is now closed; the general function of sent messenger continues.
hina ἵνα hina — in order that, so that Conjunction introducing purpose or result clauses. In final clauses it expresses deliberate design; in semi-final clauses it denotes the anticipated direction of the action toward a given result. In Romans 15:16, hina introduces the purpose of the priestly ministry: that the offering of the Gentiles might be acceptable.
olah עֹלָה olah — burnt offering, that which ascends The Levitical offering wholly consumed on the altar, illustrating propitiation — the full satisfaction of divine justice by the substitutionary death of Christ. Nothing was retained; everything ascended to God.
minchah מִנְחָה minchah — food offering, grain offering A bloodless Levitical offering of fine flour, oil, salt, and frankincense, illustrating the person of Christ in hypostatic union: sinless humanity (fine flour without leaven), the indwelling Spirit (oil), and the incorruptibility of the divine nature (salt).
shelamim שְׁלָמִים shelamim — peace offerings The Levitical fellowship offering in which God, priest, and offerer each received a portion. The shared meal across the altar illustrated reconciliation — the removal of enmity and the restoration of fellowship between the believer and God through the atoning work of Christ.
chattat חַטָּאת chattat — sin offering The Levitical offering addressing unintentional sins — transgressions committed without awareness. It illustrated divine provision for unknown sins, corresponding in the Church Age to Christ's advocacy before the Father on behalf of sins the believer has not yet named or recognized.
asham אָשָׁם asham — trespass offering, guilt offering The Levitical offering addressing specific, known transgressions against God or man, with a requirement of restitution where applicable. It illustrated the rebound principle: acknowledgment of the specific sin, reliance on the atoning work of Christ, and restoration to fellowship with God.
Hypostatic union The union of full deity and true humanity in the one person of Jesus Christ, without mixture, confusion, or diminution of either nature. The Levitical food offering served as a training aid illustrating the distinct attributes of each nature.
Propitiation The satisfaction of divine justice through the substitutionary judgment of Christ on the cross. The burnt offering in the Levitical system was the primary visual training aid for this doctrine: the animal wholly consumed depicted the complete bearing of judgment by the substitute.
Rebound The instantaneous restoration of fellowship with God through the naming of known sins to God (1 John 1:9). Illustrated in the Levitical system by the trespass offering, in which the offerer acknowledged a specific transgression and relied on the substitutionary provision of the sacrifice.
Royal family of God Church Age believers as a category distinct from Old Testament believers, sharing in the unique dignity of the Lord Jesus Christ through union with him. Every member of the royal family is simultaneously a royal priest, authorized to offer spiritual sacrifices to God and to function as a priest-communicator of doctrine.

Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Eight

Romans 15:16–17 — Sanctification by the Holy Spirit; The Esprit de Corps of the Royal Family

Romans 15:16–17 “to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: that I should be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, ministering as a priest the gospel of God, so that the offering consisting of the Gentiles might have become acceptable, having been sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Therefore in Christ Jesus I keep on having an esprit de corps in those things pertaining to God.

Romans 15 concludes with Paul's extended description of his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles. The previous section established that the Gentile believer, brought into the royal family of God through the baptism of the Holy Spirit, stands on equal footing with the Jewish believer in this dispensation. Verse 16 closed with the phrase 'having been sanctified by the Holy Spirit,' and verse 17 opens with the inference drawn from that positional reality: the communicator of doctrine possesses an esprit de corps rooted in doctrine, not in personality or circumstance. Verses 18–21, to be taken up in the following chapter, will develop the modus operandi of the missionary. The present chapter completes verse 16 and expounds verse 17.

I. The Final Phrase of Romans 15:16 — Sanctified by the Holy Spirit

A. The Verb hagiazo and Its Morphology

The participial phrase concluding verse 16 centers on the perfect passive participle of hagiazō (ἁγιάζω), meaning to set apart for an unusual or sacred purpose. The form here is best rendered having been sanctified, and three grammatical features combine to fix its precise force.

First, the tense. The dramatic perfect — the rhetorical use of the intensive perfect — emphasizes with vividness and realism the existing state produced by a completed action. The emphasis falls not on the historical moment of the action but on the present, continuing reality of sanctification. The Gentile believer has been set apart, and that set-apart status is his permanent condition.

Second, the voice. The passive voice indicates that the Gentile believer receives the action from outside himself. The agent is God the Holy Spirit, acting through the baptism of the Spirit at the moment of salvation. It is by this means that the Gentile believer is brought into the royal family of God on exactly the same basis as the Jewish believer — not through Mosaic observance, not through ethnic standing, but through the sovereign ministry of the Spirit.

Third, the function of the participle. It is a modal participle, indicating the manner in which the action of the main verb is accomplished. The acceptable offering of the Gentiles is made acceptable precisely by means of this positional sanctification — the baptism of the Spirit and the resulting union with Christ.

B. The Prepositional Phrase — By the Holy Spirit

The phrase is en (ἐν) plus the locative — or here best read as the instrumental — of pneuma hagios (πνεύματι ἁγίῳ), yielding the translation by the Holy Spirit. Every member of the Trinity has a specific, non-interchangeable function in the Protocol Plan of God. God the Holy Spirit is the agent of positional sanctification, the teacher of Bible doctrine, and the enabler of the royal family honor code. His ministry is the supernatural means by which the royal family functions in a manner consistent with its aristocratic position in Christ.

The contrast with the previous dispensation is deliberate. In the dispensation of Israel, the Jewish people were the channel of divine blessing to the nations. In the Church Age, Gentiles themselves become an offering to God — members of the royal family who, through maturity and the function of the honor code, glorify the Lord at the highest level available to any dispensation.

II. Romans 15:17 — The Esprit de Corps of the Communicator

A. The Inferential Conjunction and the Progressive Present

Verse 17 opens with the inferential post-positive conjunctive particle oun (οὖν), correctly rendered therefore. The inference is drawn from the entire preceding argument: because the Gentile believer stands in a position of full sanctification by the Holy Spirit, certain conclusions follow for the communicator of doctrine.

The main verb is the present active indicative of echō (ἔχω), to have, to hold. The present tense here is the present of duration — a retroactive progressive denoting that perception of doctrine in the past, continuing into the present, has permanent implication. Paul does not say he once had, or that he occasionally has, but that he keeps on having. The translation is therefore: Therefore I keep on having.

B. The Noun kauchēsis — Esprit de Corps

The direct object is the accusative singular of kauchēsis (καύχησις), a noun consistently rendered 'boasting' in most English translations, including the King James Version. That rendering is not wrong in itself — the root sense is confident assertion, a declaration made from a secure base — but in this context it is theologically imprecise. Kauchēsis here denotes the esprit de corps of the royal family: the inner confidence, momentum, and collective identity that flows from knowing what is essential and what is not, from being inflexible about doctrine and completely flexible in its application. It is not arrogance; it is aristocracy in function.

The King James translation — 'I have therefore whereof I may glory through Jesus Christ in those things which pertain to God' — reads as a blank check, as though any pursuit one deems spiritual qualifies. The Greek does not support this. The confidence is bounded by doctrine, defined by the honor code, and grounded in positional union with Christ. It is not a license for unchecked self-assertion.

C. In Christ Jesus — The Locative of Sphere

The prepositional phrase en Christō Iēsou (ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) establishes the sphere within which this esprit de corps exists. En plus the locative indicates that positional union with Christ is the ground of the communicator's confidence. It is not personal achievement, eloquence, or reputation that produces kauchēsis — it is the reality of being in Christ, with all the aristocratic standing that entails.

D. Those Things Pertaining to God — The Neuter Plural Demonstrative

The phrase 'in those things' translates a neuter plural definite article used as a demonstrative pronoun. The neuter gender in Greek is regularly employed to indicate abstract or doctrinal content — specifically here, Bible doctrine as the body of truth received under the grace apparatus for perception (GAP) and stored in the soul as epignōsis (ἐπίγνωσις). The demonstrative function of the article sets this content apart for special emphasis: not just any things, but those specific doctrines.

The closing prepositional phrase is pros (πρός) plus the accusative of theos (θεός), with the definite article — pros ton theon (πρὸς τὸν θεόν). The preposition with the accusative can indicate direction toward, relationship with, or pertaining to. Here the best translation is pertaining to God. The definite article with theos identifies the familiar God of Scripture, distinguishing Him from generic deity.

The full translation of verse 17 therefore reads: 'Therefore in Christ Jesus I keep on having an esprit de corps in those things pertaining to God.' The esprit de corps of the communicator — whether pastor, missionary, or teacher — is grounded not in the size of the audience, the reception of the message, or the prestige of the position, but in doctrinal norms and standards resident in the conscience of the soul.

III. The Royal Family Honor Code — Essentials and Non-Essentials

A. The Structure of the Honor Code

The royal family honor code operates on a precise distinction. The essential is doctrine — the content of Scripture as perceived, stored, and applied from the right lobe of the soul. About the essential, the mature believer is inflexible. He will not negotiate Bible doctrine, compromise its content, or adjust its demands to accommodate social pressure. Doctrine is black and white: the standard does not shift.

The non-essentials are the applications of doctrine to the infinite variety of circumstances that constitute human experience. In the non-essentials, everything operates in shades of gray. The mature believer is fully flexible here — not because he is unprincipled, but because he is operating from a single consistent principle applied differently as the situation demands. The application may appear contradictory to the observer who does not understand the underlying standard. It is not contradictory; it is aristocracy in function.

Strength through flexibility is not weakness. The believer who apologizes in one situation and refuses to back down in another, who accepts an insult without retaliation in one context and responds firmly in another, is not being inconsistent. He is operating from the essential — doctrine — while remaining completely pliable in the non-essential of application. The peasant thinker, who equates every capitulation with cowardice and every confrontation with strength, cannot understand this. Only doctrine displaces peasant thinking.

B. Arrogance as the Destroyer of Flexibility

Two conditions make genuine flexibility impossible. The first is pettiness of thought, which causes every non-essential to appear essential, filling the believer's life with perpetual conflict over trivialities. The second, and more fundamental, is arrogance. The arrogant person cannot absorb an insult, cannot allow a misunderstanding to stand uncorrected, cannot function without defending his reputation. His personal vanity becomes the lens through which every situation is read, and every situation therefore demands the same response: self-assertion, self-defense, retaliation.

The mature believer, positionally united with Christ who is King of kings and Lord of lords, has no personal hang-ups to protect. He does not need to get even. He does not need to explain himself. He does not need to prove that he was right. Those who are genuinely his friends know him and do not require explanation. Those who are his enemies would use any explanation as an additional pretext for attack. The honor code therefore requires operating from a position of inner security that renders both retaliation and self-defense unnecessary.

C. The Esprit de Corps as the Mark of the Communicator

In the context of Romans 15:17, the esprit de corps specifically characterizes the communicator of doctrine — the pastor in the pulpit, the missionary on the field, the teacher in the classroom. All three belong to the same organization: the royal family of God. All three share the same essential: Bible doctrine. All three are therefore bound by the same honor code and entitled to the same esprit de corps. The specific application differs by context and gift, but the underlying principle is identical.

This esprit de corps is not manufactured by institutional loyalty, enthusiasm, or shared hardship, though all of those may accompany it. It is produced by doctrine as the essential, resident in the soul as epignōsis, functioning through the norms and standards of the conscience, and expressed in the flexibility of daily application. When doctrine is the essential, the esprit de corps is unshakable — not because circumstances are favorable, but because the standard never changes.

IV. Looking Ahead — Romans 15:18–21

Verse 17 provides the doctrinal foundation for what follows. Romans 15:18–21 will present the modus operandi of the missionary — what a missionary actually does, how his function relates to the royal family honor code, and why the esprit de corps established in verse 17 is indispensable for effective apostolic ministry. The present chapter has established the positional basis in verse 16 (sanctification by the Holy Spirit through the baptism of the Spirit) and the operational principle in verse 17 (esprit de corps grounded in doctrine and union with Christ). These two foundations — positional and operational — will govern the entire apostolic description that follows.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Eight

1. Positional sanctification is the basis of equal standing: The perfect passive participle hagiazō in verse 16 establishes that both Jewish and Gentile believers in the Church Age are set apart by the same agent — God the Holy Spirit acting through the baptism of the Spirit at salvation. This positional sanctification is permanent and irreversible, and it constitutes the foundation for all subsequent honor code function.

2. The present of duration in verse 17 indicates sustained momentum: Paul's use of the present active indicative of echō — 'I keep on having' — signals that the esprit de corps of the communicator is not episodic but continuous. It is sustained by the ongoing intake and application of doctrine, not by favorable circumstances or recognition.

3. Kauchēsis denotes esprit de corps, not arrogant self-promotion: The noun kauchēsis, frequently rendered 'boasting,' carries in this context the technical sense of the inner confidence and collective identity of the royal family — the aristocratic assurance that flows from knowing what is essential and functioning accordingly. It is the opposite of arrogance, which is rooted in self and destroyed by reversal. True kauchēsis is rooted in union with Christ and is therefore stable.

4. The neuter plural demonstrative specifies doctrine as the content of esprit de corps: The phrase 'those things pertaining to God' uses the neuter plural definite article as a demonstrative to identify Bible doctrine — epignōsis stored in the soul — as the specific content that produces and sustains the communicator's confidence. Esprit de corps divorced from doctrinal content degenerates into institutional pride.

5. The essential/non-essential distinction is the operational key of the honor code: Inflexibility about doctrine as the essential, combined with complete flexibility in the application of doctrine to non-essentials, is the defining characteristic of spiritual aristocracy. Arrogance and pettiness each independently destroy this capacity. Only sustained doctrine intake, through the grace apparatus for perception, displaces peasant thinking and produces the flexibility that constitutes strength.

6. Every member of the Trinity has a distinct and non-interchangeable function: The phrase 'by the Holy Spirit' in verse 16 reflects the consistent pattern of the Protocol Plan of God: God the Father plans, God the Son executes redemption, and God the Holy Spirit applies the results to the believer — including positional sanctification, the teaching ministry of doctrine, and the enabling of the honor code in daily life.

7. Romans 15:18–21 will present the modus operandi of the missionary: Verse 17 functions as the doctrinal hinge between Paul's description of the Gentile offering (verse 16) and his account of apostolic methodology (verses 18–21). The esprit de corps established in verse 17 — grounded in positional union with Christ and in doctrinal norms resident in the soul — is the prerequisite for understanding what a missionary actually is and does within the royal family honor code.

Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Nine

Romans 15:18 — Missionary Modus Operandi: Word, Deed, and the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 15:18 “For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed,” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For I will not presume to speak about anything except what Christ has accomplished through me, resulting in obedience of the Gentiles, by word and by occupation.

Romans 15 continues Paul's extended treatment of the missionary calling and its requirements. Verse 18 opens with a statement of apostolic humility that is simultaneously a programmatic description of the missionary enterprise: its motivation, its method, and its scope. The verse requires careful attention to Greek idiom before its meaning can be established, and its implications extend well beyond Paul's personal experience to the governing principles of all legitimate missionary activity in the Church Age.

I. Seven Keys to Missionary Function

Before turning to the exegesis of verse 18, the broader context of missionary activity established in Romans 15 requires orientation. Missionary function in the Church Age rests on seven governing principles.

1. Communication

Communication is the primary operational requirement of missionary work. Language barriers, cultural barriers, and geographical barriers must all be overcome. The linguistic task alone is formidable: the missionary must learn not only the language of the target people but its idiom. Some of the most significant scholarly and missionary contributions in history have been made by men who devoted their entire lives to mastering a previously unwritten language, reducing it to writing, and then translating the Scriptures from the original Hebrew and Greek into that language. Communication of doctrine — whether the gospel to the unbeliever or systematic teaching to the believer — is the irreducible core of missionary work.

2. Strategy

The Lord directs missionaries only to areas where positive volition exists. A mission field is properly defined as a region where there is no local church and no evangelism underway. Where local churches are established and doctrine is being communicated, the conditions that define a mission field are not present. Divine strategy pinpoints the maximum concentration of positive volition at the point of God-consciousness in a given generation and moves prepared missionaries to that location. The great missionary movements to Africa and India in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries reflect exactly this pattern. Conversely, wherever a political system is structurally hostile to the gospel, mission fields close down — a direct consequence of the negative volition that welcomed that system in the first place.

3. Preparation

The missionary requires the most extensive preparation of any servant in the Church Age. Preparation encompasses: personal salvation; advance in the plan of God through the X, Y, and Z categories of adjustment to the justice of God; recognition of spiritual gifts; academic preparation including language acquisition and cultural orientation; honor code function; and authority orientation. No dimension of preparation can be treated as optional.

4. Spiritual and Social Intercourse

By spiritual intercourse is meant the communication of the gospel and systematic doctrinal teaching. By social intercourse is meant direct personal contact with the people of the target culture. The ministry of the Lord Jesus Christ provides the model: his conversation with Nicodemus, his extended exchange with the woman at the well in Samaria, his contact with Zacchaeus, his attendance at the wedding at Cana, his table fellowship with tax collectors, and his regular visits to the home of Mary, Martha, and Lazarus in Bethany. Social flexibility is not peripheral to missionary work; it is intrinsic to it.

5. Indigenous Modus Operandi

Missionary activity must operate on the principle of multiplication, not mere addition. The pattern of winning converts and moving on without training them to evangelize and teach in their own communities is a fundamental strategic error. The correct model: win converts, train them systematically in doctrine, commission the gifted among them as evangelists and pastor-teachers, establish self-sustaining and self-propagating local churches, and eventually develop indigenous schools and seminaries. The foreign missionary is a guest in the country. His long-term goal is to make himself unnecessary by training nationals to shepherd their own people. The native pastor knows the culture, the idiom, and the social framework from the inside. That knowledge is irreplaceable.

6. Objectivity

The missionary must not become entangled in the politics of the country where he serves. He takes no partisan position and does not attempt to reform the government. He does not intrude upon the customs of the people. His mandate is doctrine and spiritual function — not social reform, not the imposition of a foreign cultural template upon a host society. Any opposition on the mission field is ultimately opposition to the Lord and is therefore the Lord's battle to resolve. The missionary who grasps this is freed from taking insults personally and from reacting to opposition in the flesh, which creates the conditions under which the Lord can work and opposition can be broken down.

7. Personal Spiritual Growth

The missionary must never cease taking in doctrine, however difficult the circumstances. Spiritual growth must not stop. The isolation of the mission field — from one's culture, language, familiar relationships, and environment — intensifies every weakness and every hang-up. Only a sustained momentum of doctrinal intake and spiritual advance can supply the motivation necessary for long-term effective service. This is precisely the esprit de corps noted in verse 17: Paul's freedom from arrogance and his capacity for the work are grounded not in his own remarkable gifts but in the doctrine resident in his soul.

II. Exegesis of Romans 15:18a — The Negative Construction

The King James rendering of verse 18 is immediately problematic. The phrase "which Christ has not wrought by me" appears to say the opposite of what the context requires. The difficulty arises from a failure to recognize a Greek idiom involving the relative pronoun combined with the negative particle.

The Opening Negative — οὐ γάρ / ou gar

The verse begins with οὐ γάρ (ou gar), the post-positive explanatory conjunction gar combined with the negative ou. The conjunction is explanatory — "for" — and the negative is the first of two negatives in the verse. The King James translation correctly picks up this negative but places it awkwardly in the middle of the clause.

The Verb — τολμάω / tolmaō

The main verb is a future active indicative of τολμάω (tolmaō), meaning to dare or to presume. The nuance depends on whether the daring reflects genuine courage or reckless arrogance. In this context, where Paul is speaking of apostolic humility, the correct rendering is "to presume." The predictive future describes Paul's ongoing practice. The active voice indicates that Paul himself produces — or rather, refuses to produce — the action. The indicative mood states historical reality: Paul's grace-orientation and freedom from arrogant self-promotion are not occasional virtues but the settled posture of his ministry.

The man who possesses maximum doctrine in the soul, as the source of his esprit de corps noted in verse 17, does not presume to recount his own remarkable missionary achievements. He emphasizes instead what Christ has accomplished through him. This is the honor code in operation.

The Infinitive — λαλεῖν / lalein

The present active infinitive λαλεῖν (lalein), from λαλέω (laleō), to speak or to communicate, introduces the content of what Paul refuses to presume upon. The descriptive present indicates what is currently the pattern of his experience. The infinitive expresses a conceived result, a consequence of having doctrine in the soul: because doctrine is resident, arrogance is absent. The one person who can never afford a hang-up is the missionary.

The Indefinite Pronoun — τι / ti

The accusative neuter singular τι (ti), from the indefinite pronoun τις (tis), functions here not to express true indefiniteness but to delineate a category. The category will be defined by the relative clause that follows: the entirety of Paul's missionary experience. "For I will not presume to speak about anything" — that is, about anything within the category of his extraordinary apostolic service.

The Relative Clause — ὧν οὐ κατειργάσατο Χριστός / hōn ou katērgasato Christos

Here is the crux of the interpretive difficulty. The clause contains a second negative, οὐ (ou), combined with the relative pronoun ὧν (hōn). The literal rendering "which Christ has not accomplished" produces the opposite of the intended meaning. But ὅς (hos) plus οὐ (ou) is a recognized Greek idiom meaning "except what." This is not a double negative in the English sense. The relative pronoun combined with the negative particle forms an idiomatic expression of exception. The correct translation is therefore: "except what Christ has accomplished."

The verb κατειργάσατο (katērgasato) is the aorist middle indicative of κατεργάζομαι (katergazomai), meaning to achieve, to accomplish, to work out, to bring about. It is a deponent verb — middle in form but active in meaning. Christ is the subject; Christ produces the action. The constative aorist contemplates the entirety of Paul's missionary activity up to the point of writing — approximately half of his total service — as a unified whole. The indicative mood affirms historical reality: Christ has accomplished a great deal through Paul.

The final prepositional phrase δι᾽ ἐμοῦ (di' emou), διά (dia) plus the genitive of ἐγώ (egō), means "through me." Paul is the instrument; Christ is the agent. Corrected translation of the first half of verse 18: "For I will not presume to speak about anything, except what Christ has accomplished through me."

III. Exegesis of Romans 15:18b — Obedience of the Gentiles

The Result Clause — εἰς ὑπακοήν / eis hypakoēn

A prepositional phrase follows: εἰς ὑπακοήν (eis hypakoēn). Εἰς (eis) plus the accusative introduces a result clause. ὑπακοή (hypakoē) means obedience. The result of what Christ has accomplished through Paul is obedience. This obedience is not coerced conformity but the full range of response to the plan of God: salvation adjustment to the justice of God in the X category, maturity adjustment in the Y category, and the perpetuation of maturity in the Z category. The missionary's goal is not merely to secure initial conversions but to bring converts through to spiritual maturity. Quality of missionary service, not quantity of converts, is the governing standard.

The Recipients — ἐθνῶν / ethnōn

The subjective genitive plural ἐθνῶν (ethnōn), from ἔθνος (ethnos), translated "Gentiles" or "nations," identifies the scope of Paul's missionary mandate. By the time of writing, Paul has completed two missionary journeys — roughly half of his total service. His mission field encompasses the Gentile populations of the Roman world: Spain, Gaul, Italy, Asia Minor, the Middle East, Syria, Arabia, and North Africa.

By Word — λόγῳ / logō

The instrumental singular λόγῳ (logō), from λόγος (logos), here designates doctrinal communication — the primary content of missionary work. Communication of doctrine to the unbeliever is the gospel; communication of doctrine to the believer is systematic teaching. Paul was equipped for communication in at least three languages — Hebrew from his training in Jerusalem, Greek from his education in Tarsus, and Latin as a Roman citizen — supplemented in more remote settings by the gift of tongues, which provided access to languages beyond the reach of his formal education. Doctrine must come first.

By Occupation — ἔργῳ / ergō

The instrumental singular ἔργῳ (ergō), from ἔργον (ergon), means deed, action, or in this context, occupation — the professional function of the missionary. Whether the missionary's role involves evangelism, teaching, translation, church planting, school founding, or administration, it is a professional calling requiring professional execution. Professionalism means objectivity, discipline, the suppression of personal hang-ups, and the subordination of individual temperament to the requirements of the task. Administration is an intrinsic component of occupation; it cannot be separated from communication without crippling both.

IV. The Honor Code and Missionary Flexibility

The statement "I will not presume to speak about anything except what Christ has accomplished through me" is Paul's application of the Royal Family Honor Code. The mature believer has learned to distinguish the essential from the non-essential: inflexible on the essentials of doctrine, totally flexible on the non-essentials of cultural life. This combination of doctrinal rigidity and cultural flexibility is not a pragmatic compromise — it is the fruit of spiritual advance.

The mission field intensifies every personal weakness. A believer who has unresolved hang-ups connected to arrogance, cultural superiority, or legalistic taboos will find those hang-ups amplified under the pressures of isolation, unfamiliarity, and the constant scrutiny of a host culture. Inflexibility in non-essential cultural matters — dietary customs, hospitality conventions, social habits — not only fails to commend the gospel but actively discredits it by replacing the message of grace with the imposition of a foreign cultural template.

The opposite of hang-up-driven inflexibility is not moral indifference. It is the grace-orientation of the mature believer who understands what belongs to doctrine and what belongs to culture, and who can engage a host culture on its own terms without compromising the content of the message. Flexibility with humility — the product of sustained doctrinal intake and spiritual advance — is the essential personal qualification for the mission field.

V. Administration as an Integral Dimension of Missionary Occupation

A persistent failure in missionary practice has been the tendency to prioritize direct evangelism and teaching while neglecting the administrative infrastructure that makes sustained ministry possible. This is not a minor operational deficiency; it is a structural error that undermines both the communication of doctrine and the development of indigenous churches.

The indigenous modus operandi — multiplication rather than addition — requires administration at every stage: the organization of teaching programs, the selection and training of national leaders, the management of resources, the coordination of personnel, and the eventual transition of leadership to the national church. A self-sustaining local church must have not only a trained pastor-teacher but the organizational capacity to function independently of foreign support. That capacity does not arise spontaneously. It must be built, and building it requires exactly the kind of careful, systematic administrative work that field missionaries routinely find less appealing than direct proclamation.

The historical record confirms the principle. The most effective missionary movements in Church Age history have combined doctrinal clarity with administrative competence. Ulfilas, the apostle to the Goths, not only preached and taught but reduced the Gothic language to a written alphabet and translated the Scriptures — an administrative and scholarly achievement of the first order. Martin, Bishop of Tours, organized his missionaries with military precision, establishing a center on the Loire, training converts to evangelize and then to pastor, and deploying them systematically across an evangelized region before moving them on. Patrick in Ireland combined extraordinary evangelistic energy with the organizational capacity to sustain a movement that generated lasting indigenous churches and eventually shaped the trajectory of medieval Christian mission. In each case, the administration served the doctrine.

VI. Historical Survey: Mission Centers of the Early Church

Paul did not originate the missionary enterprise. It began on the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem, which served briefly as the initial center for worldwide mission before legalism throttled the congregation's outward thrust. Antioch succeeded Jerusalem as the cosmopolitan base from which Paul launched his missionary journeys. From Antioch, missionaries reached Constantinople, Persia, India, and apparently China within the first two centuries of the Church Age.

Ephesus became the next major missionary center, shaped by the successive labors of Paul and John. Alexandria in Egypt, as a great intellectual center, produced aggressive missionary outreach and some of the most influential teachers of the early centuries — Clement, Origen, and others associated with the Alexandrian school. Carthage, rebuilt on the site of the Punic city, became a remarkable center for missionary training, associated with Tertullian, Cyprian, and Augustine. Pantaenus traveled to India as a missionary in approximately 180 AD.

The testimony of writers from the first three centuries confirms the extraordinary geographical reach of early Christian missions. Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, observed that there was no people — Greek or barbarian, nomadic or settled — among whom prayers and thanksgivings were not offered in the name of Jesus Christ. Tertullian, in the following generation, wrote that Christians had already filled the cities, islands, camps, palaces, senate houses, and public forums of the Roman world. Origen noted that in both the Greek world and among barbarian peoples, tens of thousands had left their ancestral laws and gods for the law of Moses and the word of Jesus Christ, at personal cost and at risk of death. Christianity was not geographically confined to the Mediterranean basin. It reached India and China in the first two centuries.

The divergence between the Eastern and Western Churches after the division of the Empire in the fourth century is instructive. The Eastern Church at Constantinople became absorbed in doctrinal controversy and faction; missionary thrust ceased almost immediately. The Western Church, motivated by doctrine, remained vigorous for centuries: Ulfilas to the Goths, Martin of Tours to Gaul, Patrick to Ireland, Columba to Scotland, Augustine of Canterbury to Britain, and a succession of missionaries extending through the medieval period and beyond. The pattern is consistent: where doctrine is taught and received, missionary motivation follows; where doctrine is neglected or abandoned, missionary activity collapses.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Nine

1. The honor code governs missionary communication. Paul's refusal to presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through him is not false modesty. It is the application of the Royal Family Honor Code by a believer who has advanced to the point where doctrine — not personal achievement — is the center of gravity. No missionary should go to the field to prove something to anyone. The motivation must be positive volition and doctrinal content.

2. Administration is inseparable from missionary occupation. The instrumental

2. Administration cannot be neglected on the mission field. The instrumental phrase "by occupation" encompasses the full professional function of the missionary, including systematic administration. Just as a military force cannot operate without its logistical and quartermaster systems, a missionary enterprise cannot sustain itself without competent administration. Communication of doctrine and administration of structure are not competing priorities; they are mutually dependent.

3. Gentile obedience encompasses the full range of adjustment to the justice of God. The result clause "resulting in obedience" is not limited to initial salvation. It encompasses the X category (salvation adjustment), the Y category (maturity adjustment), and the Z category (perpetuation of maturity). The missionary's mandate extends from the moment of the new birth to the full realization of spiritual maturity in the believer's life.

4. Missionary function is structured by the divine equation X plus Y plus Z. Every phase of missionary work — evangelism, doctrinal teaching, pastoral training, church establishment, and the development of indigenous self-sustaining congregations — corresponds to the framework of adjustment to the justice of God. This applies to both Jewish and Gentile contexts. Paul himself, a Jew, is the divinely appointed channel to the Gentiles.

5. Paul as missionary is the instrument; Christ is the agent. The preposition "through me" is precisely chosen. Paul is not the source of missionary achievement but the instrument through which Christ acts. This understanding is the structural basis for the honor code application in the verse: because Paul knows that Christ is the agent, he has no basis for arrogant self-promotion and no inclination toward it.

6. Occupation implies professional administration under the indigenous modus operandi. The term "occupation" used to translate

6. Occupation implies professionalism under the indigenous modus operandi. Whatever the specific role of the missionary — evangelist, teacher, translator, church planter, school founder, or administrator — it must be executed with professionalism: objectivity, freedom from personal hang-ups, suppression of arrogance, and consistent focus on the mission rather than on personal reputation or cultural comfort.

7. National believers must be trained in both doctrine and administration. The indigenous principle requires that converted nationals be trained not only in systematic theology for evangelism and pastoral work, but also in the administrative competencies necessary for a self-sustaining local church. A congregation that can proclaim the gospel but cannot manage its own affairs will remain indefinitely dependent on foreign support — the opposite of the indigenous goal.

8. Paul's missionary work set the pattern for all subsequent Church Age missions. The New Testament policy established by Paul's Gentile mission was taken up by Ignatius, Polycarp, and Justin Martyr in the apostolic and post-apostolic generations, and continued through Ulfilas, Martin of Tours, Patrick, Columba, Augustine of Canterbury, Willibrord, Boniface, Ansgar, Cyril and Methodius, Raymond Lull, Zinzendorf, Roger Williams, John Eliot, and the great missionaries of subsequent centuries. In every case, effective mission was grounded in doctrine and executed with administrative competence.
